extraction.body: Nothing is preparing to unveil its first AI-native device on December 8, with new teaser images revealing a compact, screenless gadget that could function as an AI-powered voice recorder and personal assistant. The British technology company, led by CEO Carl Pei, has confirmed the launch date but remains tight-lipped about the product’s name, capabilities and pricing. Recent images show a small device with a brushed metal finish, a large button labelled “Talk” and a second button featuring a recording symbol. Red and green LED indicators are also visible, suggesting the device could be designed to capture conversations, record notes and process spoken information using artificial intelligence. Nothing has promoted the upcoming product with the tagline “Be present. It’s noted”, adding to speculation that it will focus on AI-assisted note-taking and productivity. Pei has previously argued that one of the biggest problems facing current AI technology is what he describes as the “context gap”. While AI models are becoming increasingly sophisticated, he believes they lack sufficient information about users’ daily activities, conversations and interactions. For example, an idea discussed during a casual meeting or coffee break may never reach an AI assistant because it was not captured digitally. Nothing’s upcoming device appears designed to address this limitation by providing a dedicated way to record and potentially organise information throughout the day. Unlike rival companies developing AI-powered glasses, pendants and wearable pins, Nothing is positioning its first AI product as a productivity device rather than a potential smartphone replacement. Pei has also suggested that productivity applications will be among the first areas where dedicated AI hardware delivers meaningful benefits. The Nothing CEO has confirmed that the product will have “no new screen” and said its functionality could not simply have been delivered through a smartphone application. However, the company has not revealed whether the device will operate independently, connect to a smartphone or rely on cloud-based AI processing. Questions also remain about battery life, storage, privacy features and whether recorded conversations will be processed locally or uploaded to external servers. Nothing has confirmed that the device will begin shipping in December, although specific release dates and Australian availability have yet to be announced. The December 8 unveiling will provide the first detailed look at Nothing’s plans to expand beyond smartphones and audio products into dedicated AI hardware. It is not clear if December 8 will feature a full-scale launch event or smaller online reveal, but more teasers are likely to come in the weeks ahead.

CEO Carl Pei frames it as a productivity tool meant to close the gap between capable AI models and a user's daily life. Nothing will unveil its first AI-native product on December 8, the company announced. The device has no screen. Nothing has not named it. Its tagline reads "Be present. It's noted." Nothing CEO Carl Pei confirmed earlier this month that the product would arrive in December. Teasers since then show a small brushed-metal gadget with a large "Talk" button, a second button bearing a record symbol, and red and green status LEDs. The design points to AI-powered note-taking, though Nothing has not confirmed the device's function. Pei has said AI's biggest limitation is the "context gap." Models are capable, but they lack knowledge of a user's day. An idea mentioned over coffee does not reach them. He expects AI to gain traction in productivity first, so the device targets work, not the "iPhone of AI" that rivals chase through pins, pendants and glasses. Pei offered two concrete details: the device has "no new screen" and "couldn't have been an app." The first suggests the hardware does its own processing. The second implies capture or on-device work an app could not handle. Both points remain speculation until the unveiling. Pei said the device ships in December, so sales should follow the unveiling. Nothing has not announced pricing, availability or the product name. extraction.body: Nothing is preparing to unveil its first AI-native device on December 8, with new teaser images revealing a compact, screenless gadget that could function as an AI-powered voice recorder and personal assistant. The British technology company, led by CEO Carl Pei, has confirmed the launch date but remains tight-lipped about the product’s name, capabilities and pricing. Recent images show a small device with a brushed metal finish, a large button labelled “Talk” and a second button featuring a recording symbol. Red and green LED indicators are also visible, suggesting the device could be designed to capture conversations, record notes and process spoken information using artificial intelligence. Nothing has promoted the upcoming product with the tagline “Be present. It’s noted”, adding to speculation that it will focus on AI-assisted note-taking and productivity. Pei has previously argued that one of the biggest problems facing current AI technology is what he describes as the “context gap”. While AI models are becoming increasingly sophisticated, he believes they lack sufficient information about users’ daily activities, conversations and interactions. For example, an idea discussed during a casual meeting or coffee break may never reach an AI assistant because it was not captured digitally. Nothing’s upcoming device appears designed to address this limitation by providing a dedicated way to record and potentially organise information throughout the day. Unlike rival companies developing AI-powered glasses, pendants and wearable pins, Nothing is positioning its first AI product as a productivity device rather than a potential smartphone replacement. Pei has also suggested that productivity applications will be among the first areas where dedicated AI hardware delivers meaningful benefits. The Nothing CEO has confirmed that the product will have “no new screen” and said its functionality could not simply have been delivered through a smartphone application. However, the company has not revealed whether the device will operate independently, connect to a smartphone or rely on cloud-based AI processing. Questions also remain about battery life, storage, privacy features and whether recorded conversations will be processed locally or uploaded to external servers. Nothing has confirmed that the device will begin shipping in December, although specific release dates and Australian availability have yet to be announced. The December 8 unveiling will provide the first detailed look at Nothing’s plans to expand beyond smartphones and audio products into dedicated AI hardware. passages: US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned on Sunday that further technology outages may occur as companies and government agencies modernize their systems and strengthen cybersecurity, following recent disruptions affecting air travel, banking and Microsoft services.

extraction.body: US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned on Sunday that further technology outages may occur as companies and government agencies modernize their systems and strengthen cybersecurity, following recent disruptions affecting air travel, banking and Microsoft services. Speaking on CNN's "State of the Union," Clayton said Americans should prepare for temporary interruptions as organizations invest in upgrading their infrastructure to adapt to advances in artificial intelligence (AI). "The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road," Clayton said. He added that system upgrades could lead to temporary service interruptions, saying companies and government agencies were addressing the challenges proactively. Recent disruptions involving the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Microsoft Outlook and JPMorgan affected air travel, digital services and banking transactions. However, officials have largely dismissed the possibility that the incidents were connected to a coordinated cyberattack or an attack involving artificial intelligence, noting that the disruptions had different underlying causes. The warning comes as Delta Air Lines flights faced widespread delays across the US on Sunday after a technical issue disrupted operations at the airline's main hub in Atlanta, according to local media reports and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The FAA initially imposed a ground stop for Delta flights heading to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport before replacing it with a ground delay program, local outlet Atlanta News First reported. The ground delay allowed flights bound for Atlanta to depart but resulted in average delays of nearly an hour. The program was initially expected to remain in effect until at least 1 pm local time (1800GMT). Delta attributed the disruption to a malfunction in its automated system for calculating aircraft weight and balance before departure. “Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said.​​​​​​​

extraction.body: US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned on Sunday that further technology outages may occur as companies and government agencies modernize their systems and strengthen cybersecurity, following recent disruptions affecting air travel, banking and Microsoft services. Speaking on CNN's "State of the Union," Clayton said Americans should prepare for temporary interruptions as organizations invest in upgrading their infrastructure to adapt to advances in artificial intelligence (AI). "The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road," Clayton said. He added that system upgrades could lead to temporary service interruptions, saying companies and government agencies were addressing the challenges proactively. Recent disruptions involving the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Microsoft Outlook and JPMorgan affected air travel, digital services and banking transactions. However, officials have largely dismissed the possibility that the incidents were connected to a coordinated cyberattack or an attack involving artificial intelligence, noting that the disruptions had different underlying causes. The warning comes as Delta Air Lines flights faced widespread delays across the US on Sunday after a technical issue disrupted operations at the airline's main hub in Atlanta, according to local media reports and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The FAA initially imposed a ground stop for Delta flights heading to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport before replacing it with a ground delay program, local outlet Atlanta News First reported. The ground delay allowed flights bound for Atlanta to depart but resulted in average delays of nearly an hour. The program was initially expected to remain in effect until at least 1 pm local time (1800GMT). Delta attributed the disruption to a malfunction in its automated system for calculating aircraft weight and balance before departure. “Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said.​​​​​​​

Kress noted that Nvidia's suppliers and partners are all behind it, and that it has secured the necessary memory and packaging to resume business as normal. She called out Taiwan Semi specifically, saying, "I see right now the leadership even from TSMC that was in our offices just this week, also fully engaged in helping us." While Nvidia accounts for 22% of TSMC's revenue, it's been demanding capacity that could go to other players. In the third quarter, high-performance computing, which is where AI is, accounted for 68% of total revenue, up 22% from last year. The company's broad diversification is one of the features I always point out, and here is a live example of why that's critical. TSMC is a foundry that works with many partner clients globally. It makes semiconductors for all kinds of industries, which is why it can continue to grow even as tech trends and leaders change. There's no reason to panic about Nvidia's dominant position at this time, but whoever is in the lead will likely work with TSMC. The company's new Arizona location provides greater capacity and helps it avoid tariffs. It also keeps it closer to its U.S. clients. It still has major expansion plans, including more buildings at the Arizona facility, and it has a location in Washington. Nvidia chips drive AI development, since the hyperscalers use its best-in-class chips. The new Vera Rubin system, which includes chips and computers, is in high demand. But TSMC plays an important role in making that happen, since it has the capacity to keep the chips coming. CEO C.C. Wei noted that there are several approaches to AI development right now, but since TSMC has "technology leadership, manufacturing excellence, global capacity expansion, and customer trust," all the players partner with it. Management repeated that "a higher level of capital expenditures is always correlated with higher growth opportunities in the following years." If AI does slow down, Taiwan Semi might, too. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) delivered incredible results for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 (which ended on Oct. 25) and, more importantly, raised its revenue guidance for fiscal 2028. The company's co-founder Jensen Huang recently resigned as CEO, and Nvidia is now in the hunt for a new one. Even better, Nvidia has raised its fiscal 2028 revenue guidance to 75%, up from the prior expectation of 70%. So, I won't be surprised to see this artificial intelligence (AI) specialist go on a bull run once again. But if you're still on the sidelines about Nvidia's prospects, it may be a good idea to take a closer look at another semiconductor stock -- ASML Holding (NASDAQ:ASML). Here's why. Nvidia's impressive data center growth in the previous quarter was driven by the incredible demand for its latest-generation Vera Rubin chip systems. The company noted that the Vera Rubin platform generated almost $20 billion in revenue last quarter, "making it the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history." The company noted that Rubin deployments will continue improving in 2027. Moreover, Nvidia management remarked that demand for its chips is outpacing supply. All this bodes well for ASML Holding, which manufactures the advanced chipmaking equipment that enables Nvidia to make the advanced Blackwell and Vera Rubin processors. Nvidia's Vera Rubin chip is built on a 3-nanometer (nm) process node, while the previous-generation Blackwell architecture, which remains in solid demand, is built on a 4-nm process node. These small process nodes are manufactured using extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, and ASML holds a near monopoly in this market. Not surprisingly, ASML has seen a significant increase in demand for its lithography machines. The company sold 113 new lithography systems in the third quarter of 2026, up from 66 in the year-ago period. As demand for advanced AI chips exceeds supply, ASML is looking to increase the production capacity of its EUV lithography machines. The company aims to increase the production of machines that make advanced chips by 30% in 2027. What's more, it is exploring the possibility of enhancing capacity by more than 30% in 2028. ASML management noted on the October earnings call : Our leading edge high volume customers are sharing very good visibility, as a result of the increasing number of long-term commitments they are securing with their customers. This diversified customer base means that ASML stands to gain from both the foundry/logic and memory markets, making it a safer bet than Nvidia. All this bodes well for ASML Holding, which manufactures the advanced chipmaking equipment that enables Nvidia to make the advanced Blackwell and Vera Rubin processors. Nvidia's Vera Rubin chip is built on a 3-nanometer (nm) process node, while the previous-generation Blackwell architecture, which remains in solid demand, is built on a 4-nm process node. These small process nodes are manufactured using extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, and ASML holds a near monopoly in this market. Not surprisingly, ASML has seen a significant increase in demand for its lithography machines. The company sold 113 new lithography systems in the third quarter of 2026, up from 66 in the year-ago period. Investors like to avoid uncertainty, although no one ever knows what will happen next; the entire episode was unexpected. However, some companies have tried-and-true businesses that can withstand rigorous investor scrutiny, minimizing their risk. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. No one knows what Nvidia will look like without Jensen Huang at its helm, and CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress has said that deals that resemble "circular financing" will be toned down. The changes in business approach could impact the company's financials, although Kress assured investors that demand is high, and she raised the fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook from 70% to 75%. "Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing." She said on Nvidia's 2027 third-quarter (ended Oct. 25) earnings call, "Our customers and our partners are with us... Nvidia is its largest client, overtaking Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) in importance, and one of the main beneficiaries of TSMC's expansion to Arizona, its first U.S.-based facility. Kress noted that Nvidia's suppliers and partners are all behind it, and that it has secured the necessary memory and packaging to resume business as normal. She called out Taiwan Semi specifically, saying, "I see right now the leadership even from TSMC that was in our offices just this week, also fully engaged in helping us." TSMC stock is still up 19% year-to-date, outperforming the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) , even though it's 25% off its high. While Nvidia and TSMC's success are to some degree tied together, TSMC had an excellent business before Nvidia, and it can maintain a strong business even if Nvidia does slow down. While Nvidia accounts for 22% of TSMC's revenue, it's been demanding capacity that could go to other players. In the third quarter, high-performance computing, which is where AI is, accounted for 68% of total revenue, up 22% from last year. The company's broad diversification is one of the features I always point out, and here is a live example of why that's critical. TSMC is a foundry that works with many partner clients globally. It makes semiconductors for all kinds of industries, which is why it can continue to grow even as tech trends and leaders change. There's no reason to panic about Nvidia's dominant position at this time, but whoever is in the lead will likely work with TSMC. The company's new Arizona location provides greater capacity and helps it avoid tariffs. It also keeps it closer to its U.S. clients. It still has major expansion plans, including more buildings at the Arizona facility, and it has a location in Washington. Nvidia chips drive AI development, since the hyperscalers use its best-in-class chips. The new Vera Rubin system, which includes chips and computers, is in high demand. But TSMC plays an important role in making that happen, since it has the capacity to keep the chips coming. CEO C.C. Wei noted that there are several approaches to AI development right now, but since TSMC has "technology leadership, manufacturing excellence, global capacity expansion, and customer trust," all the players partner with it. It was lower sequentially due to higher costs and growth investments. Management repeated that "a higher level of capital expenditures is always correlated with higher growth opportunities in the following years." If AI does slow down, Taiwan Semi might, too. It's not a sure thing, but even if it does happen, it isn't likely to last. By Harsh Chauhan – Nov 22, 2026 at 4:14AM EST
Nvidia ( NVDA -14.01% ) delivered incredible results for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 (which ended on Oct. 25) and, more importantly, raised its revenue guidance for fiscal 2028.

Nvidia's financial performance and outlook should come as a relief for investors during a difficult time. The company's co-founder Jensen Huang recently resigned as CEO, and Nvidia is now in the hunt for a new one. However, comments from interim CEO Colette Kress on the latest earnings call clearly suggest that the company's growth prospects remain solid.

Nvidia's revenue increased by 103% year-over-year last quarter to $115.8 billion, driven by a 110% jump in data center revenue. The company anticipates $130 billion in revenue for the current quarter, an improvement of 91% over the year-ago quarter. Even better, Nvidia has raised its fiscal 2028 revenue guidance to 75%, up from the prior expectation of 70%.

So, I won't be surprised to see this artificial intelligence (AI) specialist go on a bull run once again. But if you're still on the sidelines about Nvidia's prospects, it may be a good idea to take a closer look at another semiconductor stock -- ASML Holding ( ASML -6.63% ) . Here's why.

Nvidia's impressive data center growth in the previous quarter was driven by the incredible demand for its latest-generation Vera Rubin chip systems. The company noted that the Vera Rubin platform generated almost $20 billion in revenue last quarter, "making it the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history."

The company noted that Rubin deployments will continue improving in 2027. Moreover, Nvidia management remarked that demand for its chips is outpacing supply. All this bodes well for ASML Holding, which manufactures the advanced chipmaking equipment that enables Nvidia to make the advanced Blackwell and Vera Rubin processors.

Nvidia's Vera Rubin chip is built on a 3-nanometer (nm) process node, while the previous-generation Blackwell architecture, which remains in solid demand, is built on a 4-nm process node. These small process nodes are manufactured using extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, and ASML holds a near monopoly in this market.

Not surprisingly, ASML has seen a significant increase in demand for its lithography machines. The company sold 113 new lithography systems in the third quarter of 2026, up from 66 in the year-ago period. As demand for advanced AI chips exceeds supply, ASML is looking to increase the production capacity of its EUV lithography machines.

The company aims to increase the production of machines that make advanced chips by 30% in 2027. What's more, it is exploring the possibility of enhancing capacity by more than 30% in 2028. ASML management noted on the October earnings call :
So, ASML seems well-positioned to sustain solid long-term growth, and what makes it a better investment than Nvidia is the fact that multiple foundries and memory manufacturers use its machines.

By Jennifer Saibil – Nov 22, 2026 at 10:00PM EST 10 stocks we like better than Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing › Despite outstanding results for its latest quarter, Nvidia ( NVDA -14.01% ) stock keeps sinking. It's down 19% year-to-date, and it's clear that, for the time being, investors are concerned about what's coming up for the artificial intelligence (AI) powerhouse. Investors like to avoid uncertainty, although no one ever knows what will happen next; the entire episode was unexpected. However, some companies have tried-and-true businesses that can withstand rigorous investor scrutiny, minimizing their risk. If you're looking for a top AI company that fits the bill, consider Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM -9.48% ) . Investors are worried about Nvidia for several reasons right now. No one knows what Nvidia will look like without Jensen Huang at its helm, and CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress has said that deals that resemble "circular financing" will be toned down. The changes in business approach could impact the company's financials, although Kress assured investors that demand is high, and she raised the fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook from 70% to 75%. "Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing." She said on Nvidia's 2027 third-quarter (ended Oct. 25) earnings call, "Our customers and our partners are with us... We've got this." Many AI companies are feeling market concern, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). Nvidia is its largest client, overtaking Apple ( AAPL -1.90% ) in importance, and one of the main beneficiaries of TSMC's expansion to Arizona, its first U.S.-based facility. Kress noted that Nvidia's suppliers and partners are all behind it, and that it has secured the necessary memory and packaging to resume business as normal. She called out Taiwan Semi specifically, saying, "I see right now the leadership even from TSMC that was in our offices just this week, also fully engaged in helping us." TSMC stock is still up 19% year-to-date, outperforming the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -3.70% ) , even though it's 25% off its high. While Nvidia and TSMC's success are to some degree tied together, TSMC had an excellent business before Nvidia, and it can maintain a strong business even if Nvidia does slow down. While Nvidia accounts for 22% of TSMC's revenue, it's been demanding capacity that could go to other players. In the third quarter, high-performance computing, which is where AI is, accounted for 68% of total revenue, up 22% from last year. The company's broad diversification is one of the features I always point out, and here is a live example of why that's critical. TSMC is a foundry that works with many partner clients globally. It makes semiconductors for all kinds of industries, which is why it can continue to grow even as tech trends and leaders change. There's no reason to panic about Nvidia's dominant position at this time, but whoever is in the lead will likely work with TSMC. The company's new Arizona location provides greater capacity and helps it avoid tariffs. It also keeps it closer to its U.S. clients. It still has major expansion plans, including more buildings at the Arizona facility, and it has a location in Washington. Nvidia chips drive AI development, since the hyperscalers use its best-in-class chips. The new Vera Rubin system, which includes chips and computers, is in high demand. But TSMC plays an important role in making that happen, since it has the capacity to keep the chips coming. CEO C.C. Wei noted that there are several approaches to AI development right now, but since TSMC has "technology leadership, manufacturing excellence, global capacity expansion, and customer trust," all the players partner with it. Performance has been fantastic, fueled by AI. Sales increased 41% year over year (currency-neutral) in the third quarter, and gross margin improved by 6.9 percentage points. It was lower sequentially due to higher costs and growth investments. Management repeated that "a higher level of capital expenditures is always correlated with higher growth opportunities in the following years." If AI does slow down, Taiwan Semi might, too. It's not a sure thing, but even if it does happen, it isn't likely to last. At the current price, TSMC stock trades at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 23, which is a fantastic deal on a growth stock that will continue to drive AI development and other technology. She called out Taiwan Semi specifically, saying, "I see right now the leadership even from TSMC that was in our offices just this week, also fully engaged in helping us."
TSMC stock is still up 19% year-to-date, outperforming the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -3.70% ) , even though it's 25% off its high.

While Nvidia and TSMC's success are to some degree tied together, TSMC had an excellent business before Nvidia, and it can maintain a strong business even if Nvidia does slow down. Wei noted that there are several approaches to AI development right now, but since TSMC has "technology leadership, manufacturing excellence, global capacity expansion, and customer trust," all the players partner with it.

Performance has been fantastic, fueled by AI. Sales increased 41% year over year (currency-neutral) in the third quarter, and gross margin improved by 6.9 percentage points. If AI does slow down, Taiwan Semi might, too. It's not a sure thing, but even if it does happen, it isn't likely to last.

extraction.body: Volunteers in black uniforms and body armour increasingly seen with figures such as Tommy Robinson There is a worrying rise in “reckless and intimidating” vigilantes posing as security guards around far-right figures, security experts have said. In recent months, uniformed figures wearing all black and body armour have been seen in the entourages of far-right figures including the convicted criminal Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, who goes by the name Tommy Robinson , and Paul Golding, the leader of the far-right political party Britain First. This group of “security volunteers” has also been seen at far-right protests, most recently this week in London and in Oxford, where the controversial “race philosopher” Nathan Cofnas was due to speak. They were seen scuffling with anti-racism protesters. They have also provided security for the rightwing provocateur Katie Hopkins. The ensemble calls itself British Security UK (BSUK), and says it is a volunteer-led security group. Those who join it are given all-black uniforms featuring black and white union flags, and they are not required to have any security qualifications or training. Usually security guards are asked to have a Security Industry Authority (SIA) qualification, meaning they know how to de-escalate situations, only use proportionate force and are trained in keeping members of the public safe. The website for the “security service” carries the disclaimer: “BSUK is not the police. Wearing BSUK uniform does not confer police powers. Any security services requiring an SIA licence must be carried out by appropriately licensed personnel. For emergencies, call 999.” The registered director of BSUK is Anthony Roberts, 53, who has volunteered as a security guard for Yaxley-Lennon and Golding. He wears combat trousers, a union jack-emblazoned body armour kit, and has facial tattoos. Posting on social media, he said “the police never handle the left properly … [they] let them run riot” because of “DEI training”. He said his organisation was “there to observe the police do their job, hold them accountable to the very laws we live under, and showcase the two-tier society we all live under”. He appears to share political views with those his group “protects”. He has posted on social media in favour of “remigration” and described the UK as a “playground for savages” as a result of immigration. Roberts also appears to be a supporter of the hard-right political party Restore UK and has posed for photographs with its leader, Rupert Lowe. Daniel Garnham, the general secretary of the Security Industry Federation and a police officer for 20 years, said he was concerned by the rise of “street vigilantes” disguised as legitimate security officers. “It is definitely on the rise, I put it in the category of vigilantism and people who are based in rightwing politics that want to make a point and a protest. I don’t see it as legitimate security,” he told the Guardian. “They have security in their name but it is a vigilante group.” Garnham said no one should be acting as a security officer without an SIA licence: “My concern is the people who sign up for this in a voluntary role, they aren’t covered, they aren’t trained and they do not have insurance or trade union support. These people are not trained in personal force.” Roberts has said that his group does not need to be trained or licensed, explaining: “Under UK law (Private Security Industry Act 2001), SIA licences are only required for paid/contracted security work. Genuine unpaid volunteers with an agreement of no payment or reward do not need licences.” Garnham disagreed. He argued: “It gives off the wrong message. They call themselves British Security, members of the public could be fooled into thinking they are actual security when they aren’t.” He said he thought the mass of people dressed in black and body armour could intimidate members of the public, adding: “I think the uniform they wear is intimidating, it’s all black, with masks. This organisation shouldn’t be advertising themselves as security and shouldn’t be turning up en masse at these events. It is irresponsible and absolutely reckless.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “No one is ever entitled to intimidate or incite disorder. Anyone who breaks the law will rightly face the full force of the law.” Rightwing figures have made increasing use of private security in recent years. There is no suggestion any of these security guards do not have the appropriate qualifications and training. One of Nigel Farage’s security team who accompanied him on the local election campaign trail this year was facing a rape charge and was later jailed for eight years, which raised questions around vetting within Reform UK. Roberts did not respond to a request for comment, but posted on social media after being approached: “Under the Private Security Industry Act 2001 and current SIA guidance, genuinely unpaid volunteers do not need an SIA licence, provided they have a written or spoken agreement that they will receive no payment or reward for the work. “It has come to our attention that sections of the mainstream media are preparing critical coverage of myself and my team. We are accustomed to this. Those of us who seek to contribute positively to our communities and country are frequently subjected to scrutiny that appears more interested in fitting a preferred narrative than in examining the facts.”

Asked by host Jonathan Karl in an interview on ABC News' "This Week" whether she passed information to the Chinese government, Clayton said, "There is an investigation ongoing into her firm and into her," and that he would await its outcome. He also said he did not know where Jensen Huang is. Clayton cast Nvidia as a magnet for illegal buyers. The Commerce Department began investigating the firm in 2024 for possible violations of U.S. export controls, the rules restricting sales of sensitive technology abroad, and the Justice Department later took over the criminal probe, the two agencies said in a joint statement Monday, The Hill reported . extraction.body: Trevor Campbell, Sales Development Manager of Microscopy at Zeiss Industrial Quality Solutions, discusses artificial intelligence, microscopy, and a new manufacturing report deployed by Zeiss from the MAX Show in Nashville. Michelle: Zeiss recently released its Manufacturing Insights Report, which highlighted the importance of measurement and metrology across manufacturing industries, including aerospace. Can you tell us how is metrology evolving to meet these demands? Trevor: One of the core competencies at Zeiss is that we want to be well connected with our customers. They're job number one when it comes to us handling the industry as a whole. So, recently we did a very large study with a huge population of our customers to try to get more information from them about what matters. What trends are they seeing? What are the challenges they're facing? And how can we as a quality company help them meet those demands? A pretty heavy contingent of that was in the aerospace industry, which happens to be one of my focuses at Zeiss. I lead a team of people focused on our aerospace customers. So, there's a really healthy amount of valuable information in that insights report that we've been able to learn a lot from and go back to our R&D team and make suggestions for on ways that we think we can improve our processes and in turn help their processes in the field. Michelle: Of course, the other big buzzer people are talking about is AI. So, with artificial intelligence entering manufacturing now, what specific role is AI playing in improving aerospace? Trevor: That's a good question. There's a number of different ways that we're adding to it right now. Some of them are more throughput based where we're finding ways to generate results faster. Some of that is through image reconstruction in non-destructive testing, specifically our X-ray microscope, our Versa. We can improve scan times by interpreting data as it's coming in using artificial intelligence, where it's able to blend together the different slices that it's taking faster to give you a much faster scan time and a faster time to results. There's other techniques that we use it for when it comes to pattern recognition or image analysis, both in our microscopes as well as our CT x-ray systems. On the CT x-ray side, we have a defect detection algorithm that we are able to train based off of known defects to where it can recognize those in the sample as it's finding it. So, they're automated. It's not something that somebody has to sit there and comb through a bunch of images as it's taking these x-ray slices and say, okay, that looks like a void that shouldn't be there. It's finding it in real time without the operator having to intervene at all. extraction.body: Dr. Linir Zamir, who’s been working on the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite, discusses how Artificial Intelligence is re-shaping manufacturing. AI is moving fast, and on the factory floor, that speed brings both excitement and real concern. Some workers worry it’s going to replace them. Others are interested, but hesitant, because they’ve heard about hallucinations, bad outputs and AI tools that sound great in theory but fall apart in real operations. In this conversation, we focus on the practical side: how people in the AI industry are working to make these systems more reliable, how manufacturers can use AI to strengthen the workforce they already have and what it actually looks like to deploy AI across the factory floor in a way that delivers return on investment. ASSEMBLY: Folks are fearful of AI taking over their jobs. From your perspective, what’s the most realistic way workers should think about AI? And what advice would you give to someone who’s worried it’s going to replace them? ZAMIR: It makes sense to be cautious about AI. I understand it. You hear it all over. You’ve seen the movies, and the idea of AI can be terrifying sometimes. But I think nowadays, as time progresses and we see more and more AI evolving within our daily lives—like ChatGPT—people are now using it for almost anything, even drafting an email. You can use ChatGPT. ChatGPT does not send the email, but it does help you draft a better version of it. That’s exactly the same way we think about agents in manufacturing. We’re not replacing the operator. We’re not taking the job from them. We’re giving the operator the tools to make better decisions, to understand the procedure better, and to have the right context whenever they need it. Every evolution has some cautiousness and fearfulness related to it, and it’s the same with AI. But it’s something that the more we understand, the less we’re afraid of it. We’re giving the operators—and any level of the manufacturer—the tools, but we also explain how the tool behaves. What exactly does it do? What data is being transferred between the different agents? So we don’t give just the tool by itself, but also a deeper understanding of what exactly is happening, so people can understand it and not be afraid of it. And yeah. At the end of the day, we are not replacing; we are enhancing. ASSEMBLY: In the recent past, AI has been criticized for a number of reasons. How do folks in the AI industry tackle these issues to make sure the AI agents are as foolproof as they can be? ZAMIR: I think there are two points to what you said. One of them is that up until recently, AI had the issue of what is called hallucination, where it was not as reliable. People found errors or issues. There was a famous example with ChatGPT and the number of “R’s” in the word “strawberry.” I don’t know if you’ve heard of that, but ChatGPT hallucinated 30% to 40% of the time. If we are trying to build agents for manufacturers, where every second counts and accuracy is critical, we cannot allow those hallucinations. But in the past year or so, we’ve seen tools—and the foundation models themselves—become as reliable as you can get, assuming you give them the right context, which is what we do with the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite. We provide the right context. And there’s going to be pushback on any new technology. ASSEMBLY: That’s a very good point about pushback. How do you handle that when you talk to manufacturers? ZAMIR: First of all, the quality of the language models is much better than it used to be. We are in a very close relationship with NVIDIA, as mentioned, and we are implementing some foundation models. For example, Cosmos. Cosmos is a foundation model that is designed to be specific for manufacturing, so it has a much better understanding of the environment. That’s one thing. But hallucination depends on the context that you provide to the agent, because deviceWISE has so much data. So for any question or any understanding the agent needs, we provide the proper context. And we also have MCP protocol, which allows us to provide the agents with exactly the right context they need in order to understand, make a decision, and provide the right result or output to the operator for any input it might get. Those are the ways we can essentially fix, or handle, cases of hallucination. I would say this is 99.9% hallucination-proof, but for the 0.01%, that’s why you still have the person. extraction.body: Trevor Campbell, Sales Development Manager of Microscopy at Zeiss Industrial Quality Solutions, discusses artificial intelligence, microscopy, and a new manufacturing report deployed by Zeiss from the MAX Show in Nashville. Michelle: Zeiss recently released its Manufacturing Insights Report, which highlighted the importance of measurement and metrology across manufacturing industries, including aerospace. Can you tell us how is metrology evolving to meet these demands? Trevor: One of the core competencies at Zeiss is that we want to be well connected with our customers. They're job number one when it comes to us handling the industry as a whole. So, recently we did a very large study with a huge population of our customers to try to get more information from them about what matters. What trends are they seeing? What are the challenges they're facing? And how can we as a quality company help them meet those demands? A pretty heavy contingent of that was in the aerospace industry, which happens to be one of my focuses at Zeiss. I lead a team of people focused on our aerospace customers. So, there's a really healthy amount of valuable information in that insights report that we've been able to learn a lot from and go back to our R&D team and make suggestions for on ways that we think we can improve our processes and in turn help their processes in the field. Michelle: Of course, the other big buzzer people are talking about is AI. So, with artificial intelligence entering manufacturing now, what specific role is AI playing in improving aerospace? Trevor: That's a good question. There's a number of different ways that we're adding to it right now. Some of them are more throughput based where we're finding ways to generate results faster. Some of that is through image reconstruction in non-destructive testing, specifically our X-ray microscope, our Versa. We can improve scan times by interpreting data as it's coming in using artificial intelligence, where it's able to blend together the different slices that it's taking faster to give you a much faster scan time and a faster time to results. There's other techniques that we use it for when it comes to pattern recognition or image analysis, both in our microscopes as well as our CT x-ray systems. On the CT x-ray side, we have a defect detection algorithm that we are able to train based off of known defects to where it can recognize those in the sample as it's finding it. So, they're automated. It's not something that somebody has to sit there and comb through a bunch of images as it's taking these x-ray slices and say, okay, that looks like a void that shouldn't be there. It's finding it in real time without the operator having to intervene at all. Trevor: One of the core competencies at Zeiss is that we want to be well connected with our customers. They're job number one when it comes to us handling the industry as a whole. So, recently we did a very large study with a huge population of our customers to try to get more information from them about what matters. What trends are they seeing? What are the challenges they're facing? And how can we as a quality company help them meet those demands?

A pretty heavy contingent of that was in the aerospace industry, which happens to be one of my focuses at Zeiss. I lead a team of people focused on our aerospace customers. So, there's a really healthy amount of valuable information in that insights report that we've been able to learn a lot from and go back to our R&D team and make suggestions for on ways that we think we can improve our processes and in turn help their processes in the field.
Michelle: Of course, the other big buzzer people are talking about is AI. So, with artificial intelligence entering manufacturing now, what specific role is AI playing in improving aerospace?

Trevor: That's a good question. There's a number of different ways that we're adding to it right now. Some of them are more throughput based where we're finding ways to generate results faster. Some of that is through image reconstruction in non-destructive testing, specifically our X-ray microscope, our Versa. We can improve scan times by interpreting data as it's coming in using artificial intelligence, where it's able to blend together the different slices that it's taking faster to give you a much faster scan time and a faster time to results.
There's other techniques that we use it for when it comes to pattern recognition or image analysis, both in our microscopes as well as our CT x-ray systems.

On the CT x-ray side, we have a defect detection algorithm that we are able to train based off of known defects to where it can recognize those in the sample as it's finding it. So, they're automated. It's not something that somebody has to sit there and comb through a bunch of images as it's taking these x-ray slices and say, okay, that looks like a void that shouldn't be there. It's finding it in real time without the operator having to intervene at all.

extraction.body: Dr. Linir Zamir, who’s been working on the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite, discusses how Artificial Intelligence is re-shaping manufacturing. AI is moving fast, and on the factory floor, that speed brings both excitement and real concern. Some workers worry it’s going to replace them. Others are interested, but hesitant, because they’ve heard about hallucinations, bad outputs and AI tools that sound great in theory but fall apart in real operations. In this conversation, we focus on the practical side: how people in the AI industry are working to make these systems more reliable, how manufacturers can use AI to strengthen the workforce they already have and what it actually looks like to deploy AI across the factory floor in a way that delivers return on investment. ASSEMBLY: Folks are fearful of AI taking over their jobs. From your perspective, what’s the most realistic way workers should think about AI? And what advice would you give to someone who’s worried it’s going to replace them? ZAMIR: It makes sense to be cautious about AI. I understand it. You hear it all over. You’ve seen the movies, and the idea of AI can be terrifying sometimes. But I think nowadays, as time progresses and we see more and more AI evolving within our daily lives—like ChatGPT—people are now using it for almost anything, even drafting an email. You can use ChatGPT. ChatGPT does not send the email, but it does help you draft a better version of it. That’s exactly the same way we think about agents in manufacturing. We’re not replacing the operator. We’re not taking the job from them. We’re giving the operator the tools to make better decisions, to understand the procedure better, and to have the right context whenever they need it. Every evolution has some cautiousness and fearfulness related to it, and it’s the same with AI. But it’s something that the more we understand, the less we’re afraid of it. We’re giving the operators—and any level of the manufacturer—the tools, but we also explain how the tool behaves. What exactly does it do? What data is being transferred between the different agents? So we don’t give just the tool by itself, but also a deeper understanding of what exactly is happening, so people can understand it and not be afraid of it. And yeah. At the end of the day, we are not replacing; we are enhancing. ASSEMBLY: In the recent past, AI has been criticized for a number of reasons. How do folks in the AI industry tackle these issues to make sure the AI agents are as foolproof as they can be? ZAMIR: I think there are two points to what you said. One of them is that up until recently, AI had the issue of what is called hallucination, where it was not as reliable. People found errors or issues. There was a famous example with ChatGPT and the number of “R’s” in the word “strawberry.” I don’t know if you’ve heard of that, but ChatGPT hallucinated 30% to 40% of the time. If we are trying to build agents for manufacturers, where every second counts and accuracy is critical, we cannot allow those hallucinations. But in the past year or so, we’ve seen tools—and the foundation models themselves—become as reliable as you can get, assuming you give them the right context, which is what we do with the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite. We provide the right context. And there’s going to be pushback on any new technology. ASSEMBLY: That’s a very good point about pushback. How do you handle that when you talk to manufacturers? ZAMIR: First of all, the quality of the language models is much better than it used to be. We are in a very close relationship with NVIDIA, as mentioned, and we are implementing some foundation models. For example, Cosmos. Cosmos is a foundation model that is designed to be specific for manufacturing, so it has a much better understanding of the environment. That’s one thing. But hallucination depends on the context that you provide to the agent, because deviceWISE has so much data. So for any question or any understanding the agent needs, we provide the proper context. And we also have MCP protocol, which allows us to provide the agents with exactly the right context they need in order to understand, make a decision, and provide the right result or output to the operator for any input it might get. Those are the ways we can essentially fix, or handle, cases of hallucination. I would say this is 99.9% hallucination-proof, but for the 0.01%, that’s why you still have the person. That’s why we still need the person to validate and to say, “That’s true,” or “Holds up. It’s not an issue like you think it is.” But having this person is a layer of protection. The longer you have the agent running, and the longer it can interact with a person and understand the context of the environment it resides in, the less chance there is of it making any mistake or hallucination. So yeah: the quality of the agent, the MCP or the context involved, and then the person at the end to verify that everything is accurate. That’s part of it. Like all agentic AI, there’s going to be pushback, but the way we solve that and make people believe in the technology is to show them. We are comfortable with what we bring. We know what we have, and we’ve seen success all around. Being able to put the technology on the factory floor—bringing the small hardware component that can suddenly see everything—and showing them, “Hey, listen, within a minute I can see all the temperature changes, and I can give you an evaluation of what might fault within the next week or month,” and giving them this data shows the value. Initially, they might push back a little, but once they see the results they expect to see, it becomes much easier to adopt those technologies. At the end of the day, it’s a question of money, like almost everything is. If we can help manufacturers lower cost and lower downtime—which costs them a lot of money—they will definitely be inclined to adopt that technology and use the new tools that are available nowadays. Ask ASM → ASSEMBLY: A lot of manufacturers, because of the skilled labor shortage, are having to take the teams that they already have and make the most of them. This idea of using AI to enhance the operator basically means giving the people on the plant floor tools that help them work faster, make better decisions, and solve problems more consistently, without replacing their expertise or taking them out of the process, right? ZAMIR: Yeah, definitely. And what you said, we’ve heard so many times before. Actually, even NVIDIA themselves brought this up the other day when we had a conversation with them. ASSEMBLY: Can you explain how AI programs like the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite fit into this idea? ZAMIR: The Intelligence Suite helps exactly with that situation. We can take the operator, and we can even help with the training of an operator. Instead of spending hours and taking time from other operators to teach or explain, you can have the Intelligence Suite as the source of knowledge that every operator can use to know more and to understand the process that needs to be taken, to be much more productive, to understand the concept of the factory much better, and to know exactly what steps need to be taken. So we definitely help with that specific issue that we’ve seen across all factories that we’ve worked with. ASSEMBLY: What ROI should manufacturers expect when deploying agents across the factory floor? ZAMIR: Definitely the most immediate one is downtime recovery, or time to recovery. This is by far the main focus area of what we do. We want to make sure to minimize any error or fault. And because deviceWISE Intelligence is located right between the OT we get from the robots and the IT data from the top, when you get a fault on one of the robots, deviceWISE Intelligence can immediately contact SAP or CMMS maintenance, and even order the part if needed, depending on the requirement from that manufacturer. So downtime can get significantly shorter, and that’s the goal of what we’re trying to do. That’s one of the main impacts we see. ASSEMBLY: And building on that, tell us about the idea of self-mapping factories. ZAMIR: Yeah, self-mapping factory is our vision where the software can see the factory as a living system. Instead of the engineer needing to configure every connection, if you want to swap something like a piece of hardware, it’s a process. This self-mapping factory is going to identify different PLCs, robots and sensors, and it can help you see exactly the effect of different changes you might have. We also have what is called a digital twin as part of the Intelligence Suite, which allows us to have a simulation of the real-life factory you have, where you have all the different components like the PLCs, sensors and robots. All of them reside on a digital twin that lets you see the effect of anything you might change in the real factory. In the real-life factory, if I want to add another conveyor belt, is the robot movement going to hit it by mistake? Those are questions you would not know until you tried it yourself in the real factory. Instead of doing that—where you need to buy the parts and take risks—now you can do the simulation and see how it behaves. Now you have the self-mapping factory in real life and in the simulation. It can oversee all the data it has, all the context of the factory, including the components, the location, the distances, the temperature and all of those pieces of information can be leveraged by the Intelligence Suite to find the connection between different things, or different parts, that you have in the factory. This is essentially the factory of the future. Every factory is going to eventually get to that point. You want to have a simulation of your factory so you can cut costs tremendously, and test different scenarios and replacements within this digital simulation. ASSEMBLY: How many factories are using digital twins at this moment? ZAMIR: Honestly, at first I thought it was, “Oh, it’s a cool thing to have.” It sounds nice. We were like, “Okay, let’s see. How can we integrate that? What can we do?” But the response was incredible. I would say eight out of 10 large manufacturers that we work with have some sort of digital twin implementation, and it is being adopted like crazy at so many different levels. We’ve seen factories benefit so much from those digital twins, to be able, like I mentioned, to see all the different scenarios that might occur. Everything is a question of money at the end of the day. If this digital twin can help factories lower cost because they don’t need to take chances—they can simulate everything before they act in real life—it’s cost saving. We’ve seen it adopted a lot. ASSEMBLY: While a lot of manufacturers have adopted AI at some level, a lot don’t have any deployment across the factory floor. So what advice do you have for manufacturing leaders who are looking to scale, and how does deviceWISE help with this issue in particular? ZAMIR: Again, very good question. AI is such a big umbrella. There are so many components that can be labeled as AI. There are so many options for implementing AI. The question is: what is the AI that you work with? From a high-level perspective, what we do is integrations with deviceWISE. Part of the integration is integrations with AI tools and components, which is why we are working closely with NVIDIA. But not just NVIDIA—we work with different NPU manufacturers as well. This is part of the reason we have MCP: to be more agnostic to the AI being used or deployed in different manufacturers. So I would say integrations are the key part. ASSEMBLY: A lot of folks in manufacturing are retiring or getting close to retiring. What advice do you have to manufacturing leaders who are looking for candidates to fill those roles, especially given this AI emergence? ZAMIR: Definitely, I would say the younger generation is more technology-friendly, or savvy. It’s not a requirement, but it definitely helps. It can help the operator when interacting with those different agents. We’ve done work with many factories, and the people we worked with who interacted with deviceWISE and the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite are close to retirement age. But it’s essentially like talking to ChatGPT. Even my parents use ChatGPT, and they’re close to retiring, and they can still use it. It’s easy. It’s very intuitive, it’s interactive, and you don’t need to be as technology-savvy to work with those different agents. It’s the same for the factory. So while it does help if you know a little bit more about the technology, it’s not a requirement. You can have an agent you talk to, as we’re talking right now. You can talk to the agent, and it can provide you with information in a friendly way. It can be an Excel sheet, a PDF or whatever, that you can go over and read. So yeah, it’s not a requirement. It’s good, but we want to make it as simple and intuitive as possible to interact with those different agents. Looking for a reprint of this article? passages: The race for faster data processing is pushing infrastructure to its limits, forcing a choice between specialized connectivity and massive storage.
You might be deciding between Credo Technology Group (NASDAQ:CRDO) and Western Digital (NASDAQ:WDC) for 2027.
The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.

Credo provides high-speed connectivity solutions that enable artificial intelligence data centers to communicate efficiently, while Western Digital is a global leader in both hard disk and flash storage.
While they operate in different niches, both are essential players in the scaling of cloud infrastructure.
This comparison evaluates which stock offers the best path for long-term growth.
The company sells products like Active Electrical Cables and optical components to hyperscale operators and system vendors.
It has established key partnerships with Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) to enhance connectivity for dual-architecture systems.
The company also deals with geopolitical risks due to its reliance on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company for all semiconductor manufacturing.
Furthermore, it manages previously flagged intellectual property litigation with Marvell Technology, which was recently resolved via a settlement.

Arm provides the energy-efficient architecture used in almost every smartphone, while Marvell specializes in high-speed networking and data center infrastructure.

This comparison helps you determine which path fits your investment strategy through 2027.
Marvell Technology deals with significant customer concentration and geopolitical uncertainty.
Trade restrictions and export controls regarding China have created supply chain challenges and impacted demand.

Marvell sports a much lower share price valuation than Arm, providing a greater opportunity for a superior return.
Arm arguably deserves the elevated valuation multiples because of its high-margin licensing moat.
However, given its foray into making its own semiconductor chips, it risks compressing those robust margins due to manufacturing costs.

Instead, it designs the primary architecture and licenses its intellectual property.

Bitcoin’s decline has been long and significant. Market analyst Charlie Bilello pointed out on November 21, 2026, that Bitcoin had dropped 56% from its peak to its low, marking the longest peak-to-trough decline in its history and lasting 411 days.

Despite this downturn, the $1 million target continues to generate interest. Bernstein, a Wall Street research firm, has set a long-term target of about $1 million by 2033, and long-term holders often cite it as a potential destination for Bitcoin. So, can Bitcoin still reach $1 million by 2035?

Market capitalization is the total value of a cryptocurrency, calculated by multiplying its price by the number of coins in circulation. If Bitcoin reached $1 million per coin, its market value would soar to around $20.12 trillion, up from about $1.22 trillion now. This required gain of 1,546% translates to an annual increase of roughly 36% over the 9.1 years remaining until the end of 2035.

Bitcoin’s growing supply adds another layer of difficulty to this target. When Bitcoin closed at $8,118 on November 22, 2017, its entire market cap was about $135.5 billion. Now, with approximately 20.1 million coins in circulation out of a maximum of 21 million, every dollar increase in price adds significantly more value than it did in 2017.

Reaching a market cap of $20.12 trillion would put Bitcoin in the same league as gold, a comparison supporters often use. However, gold is currently trading around $3,536 per ounce, down 33% from $5,279 at the end of February 2026, suggesting this benchmark has also declined.

passages: For Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) to reach $1 million by 2035, it must gain about 1,546%. Over the past year, this goal has become even harder to reach. Currently, Bitcoin trades around $60,763, 51.8% below its all-time high of $126,080 set on October 6, 2025. In its latest 24-hour session, its price moved between $58,696 and $61,447.

Bitcoin’s decline has been long and significant. Market analyst Charlie Bilello pointed out on November 21, 2026, that Bitcoin had dropped 56% from its peak to its low, marking the longest peak-to-trough decline in its history and lasting 411 days.

Despite this downturn, the $1 million target continues to generate interest. Bernstein, a Wall Street research firm, has set a long-term target of about $1 million by 2033, and long-term holders often cite it as a potential destination for Bitcoin. So, can Bitcoin still reach $1 million by 2035?

Market capitalization is the total value of a cryptocurrency, calculated by multiplying its price by the number of coins in circulation. If Bitcoin reached $1 million per coin, its market value would soar to around $20.12 trillion, up from about $1.22 trillion now. This required gain of 1,546% translates to an annual increase of roughly 36% over the 9.1 years remaining until the end of 2035.

Bitcoin’s growing supply adds another layer of difficulty to this target. When Bitcoin closed at $8,118 on November 22, 2017, its entire market cap was about $135.5 billion. Now, with approximately 20.1 million coins in circulation out of a maximum of 21 million, every dollar increase in price adds significantly more value than it did in 2017.

Reaching a market cap of $20.12 trillion would put Bitcoin in the same league as gold, a comparison supporters often use. However, gold is currently trading around $3,536 per ounce, down 33% from $5,279 at the end of February 2026, suggesting this benchmark has also declined.

Bernstein bases its projections on Bitcoin’s four-year cycle, which is linked to the halving, an event that reduces the reward for mining new coins roughly every four years. Under Bernstein’s main scenario, Bitcoin could reach $150,000 by mid-2027, climb to about $300,000 in 2029, and near $1 million by 2033. However, this same report anticipated Bitcoin would rebound to $125,000 by late 2026, and Bitcoin is currently trading far below that level.

Standard Chartered has a more cautious outlook. The bank pushed its $500,000 target back from 2028 to 2030 in December 2025. In April 2026, analyst Geoffrey Kendrick set a year-end price target of $100,000. Even this $100,000 goal now seems ambitious.

Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) hold Bitcoin, so their purchases pull coins off the market. SoSoValue data indicates that cumulative net inflows to spot Bitcoin ETFs fell from $57.62 billion on October 29 to $53.51 billion on November 19.

On November 19 alone, these funds recorded $582 million in net outflows, and they took in money on only six trading days between October 23 and November 19. The total net assets of Bitcoin ETFs dropped to $76.55 billion from $104.88 billion on October 28, squeezed by both outflows and declining prices.

Higher interest rates add more pressure. The federal funds rate is the benchmark for overnight loans, and higher rates typically divert investment away from speculative assets like Bitcoin. The Federal Reserve raised its upper limit to 4.00% from 3.75% in September, and markets are bracing for another possible rate hike on December 9. Kendrick has cautioned that if this tightening continues, Bitcoin could drop to about $50,000, 18% below its current price.

Since it closed at $8,118 in November 2017, Bitcoin has grown at an annual compounded rate of about 25%. While this is a strong performance for most assets, it falls short of the 36% annual growth needed to reach the $1 million target.

The last five years have shown even weaker performance. Bitcoin has risen only about 4% since November 2021, despite nearly an 8,000% increase over the past decade. Both our five-year Bitcoin outlook and our look at $1,000 in Bitcoin by 2030 illustrate how much returns have slowed.

Even Bitcoin enthusiasts predict more modest gains going forward. Investor and podcast host Anthony Pompliano remarked on August 19, 2026, “The future return of Bitcoin, I think, is going to be much lower than people have previously experienced. So I don’t think it’s going to compound at 60%, 70% year over year for a decade.”

Bitcoin’s chance of reaching $1 million by 2035 appears low. First, it must recover its all-time high of $126,080, which is 107% above the current price, as our prediction on when Bitcoin gets back there covers. Then spot ETF outflows need to turn into steady inflows, the Fed needs to stop raising rates, and Bitcoin has to compound near 36% a year, faster than it has since 2017.

Bernstein’s $150,000 mid-2027 checkpoint is the first test. If Bitcoin is still below $126,080 by mid-2027 and cumulative ETF inflows keep shrinking from $53.51 billion, the $1 million target could slip well past 2035. But if Bitcoin closes above its old high with weeks of steady ETF inflows, $1 million could return to serious conversation, though the late 2030s still look more likely.

sources.title: Debian 13.8 bundles kernel and Chromium security fixes with a 122-package bugfix list - Help Net Security
passages: The security table runs from DSA-6408 to DSA-6629 (a DSA is a Debian Security Advisory).
It covers Chromium, Firefox ESR, OpenJDK 25, nginx, BIND 9, Dovecot, rsync, PostgreSQL 17 and the Linux kernel.
Chromium is the package the table lists most often.
A second table lists 122 packages with bugfixes, among them security fixes in glibc, grub2, MariaDB, intel-microcode and sssd.
The Debian project released Debian 13.8, the eighth update to its stable “trixie” series.
It mainly carries security fixes, plus corrections for a few serious bugs, and it bundles advisories Debian had already published separately.
Existing installs get 13.8 by upgrading packages from an HTTP mirror , and old trixie install media still works.
If you already pull updates from security.debian.org often, you will find few packages left to update, since most of those fixes are already in the release.

sources.title: This Free 'Swiss Army Knife' For macOS Can Replace Your Utility Apps - Engadget
passages: macOS offers one of the most refined desktop experiences, but users looking for more granular control of their desktops might find the OS' native options limiting.

Unlike Microsoft's PowerToys , which includes a collection of over 25 productivity and customization tools, Mac users must often turn to a fragmented selection of third-party applications to achieve similar levels of control.
For example, macOS' native window tiling is serviceable at best, allowing for only a few tiling options regardless of screen size.
Similarly, the OS doesn't natively support independent volume control and output device selection for individual applications.
This is where Vorssaint, the Swiss Army Knife of macOS utility apps, comes into the picture.
The application suite also includes several handy tools that streamline daily workflows.
For example, its screenshot utility supports scrolling screenshots, which makes it possible to capture content that extends beyond what's visible on the screen.
Users can also edit captured screenshots with the app's in-built image editing tool.
Similarly, Vorssaint's media tool is capable of video compression, image conversion and text extraction from images.

passages: The app helps users discover local events, such as concerts, trivia nights, and comedy shows, while also giving them a built-in way to connect with others who plan to attend.
Instead of going to events alone, users can create or join “plans,” which are small group meetups tied to specific events.
Lauren covers media, streaming, apps and platforms at TechCrunch.
The app uses a paid membership model that varies by city, with fees of $70 in New York and €55 in Amsterdam.
The apps aim to provide a less awkward solution than, for instance, approaching a stranger at the gym or local café and trying to strike up a conversation.
These platforms clearly indicate that everyone using the app is looking for the same thing — friendship, not romance — making it much less intimidating to initiate conversations.
The app 222 is an iOS-only social events platform that facilitates in-person meetups by pairing a group of strangers based on their personality test results.
There is then a vetting process, and selected participants are notified on the day of the event.
A bonus for those who feel socially anxious: You’re allowed to bring a plus-one.
Clyx is another emerging app in the group-based social networking landscape, with a strong focus on discovering local events.
The social platform helps users find community events by integrating data from platforms like Ticketmaster and TikTok.
They can also chat with group members and post updates and photos from gatherings.
Mmotion is a newly launched friendship app that blends location tracking with social discovery to help users connect with people nearby and explore new bars and restaurants in their area.
Upon joining, users can participate in interest-based groups — such as hiking, basketball, or art — view a map of active users, and send messages to those nearby.
As of now, Clyx operates exclusively in two cities: Miami and London.
However, it has plans to expand to additional areas in the near future, with New York City and São Paulo at the top of the list.

Thanks to online dating apps, the stigma associated with finding connections online has largely faded away. This has welcomed a new wave of apps focused on fostering friendships and building local communities.

sources.title: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
passages: Lilian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F.
Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment.

On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times.
Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors.
Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history.
But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its 2024 split from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future.

A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year.
“Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch.
“It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added.

After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said.

Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025.
Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic.
