extraction.body: Trevor Campbell, Sales Development Manager of Microscopy at Zeiss Industrial Quality Solutions, discusses artificial intelligence, microscopy, and a new manufacturing report deployed by Zeiss from the MAX Show in Nashville. Michelle: Zeiss recently released its Manufacturing Insights Report, which highlighted the importance of measurement and metrology across manufacturing industries, including aerospace. Can you tell us how is metrology evolving to meet these demands? Trevor: One of the core competencies at Zeiss is that we want to be well connected with our customers. They're job number one when it comes to us handling the industry as a whole. So, recently we did a very large study with a huge population of our customers to try to get more information from them about what matters. What trends are they seeing? What are the challenges they're facing? And how can we as a quality company help them meet those demands? A pretty heavy contingent of that was in the aerospace industry, which happens to be one of my focuses at Zeiss. I lead a team of people focused on our aerospace customers. So, there's a really healthy amount of valuable information in that insights report that we've been able to learn a lot from and go back to our R&D team and make suggestions for on ways that we think we can improve our processes and in turn help their processes in the field. Michelle: Of course, the other big buzzer people are talking about is AI. So, with artificial intelligence entering manufacturing now, what specific role is AI playing in improving aerospace? Trevor: That's a good question. There's a number of different ways that we're adding to it right now. Some of them are more throughput based where we're finding ways to generate results faster. Some of that is through image reconstruction in non-destructive testing, specifically our X-ray microscope, our Versa. We can improve scan times by interpreting data as it's coming in using artificial intelligence, where it's able to blend together the different slices that it's taking faster to give you a much faster scan time and a faster time to results. There's other techniques that we use it for when it comes to pattern recognition or image analysis, both in our microscopes as well as our CT x-ray systems. On the CT x-ray side, we have a defect detection algorithm that we are able to train based off of known defects to where it can recognize those in the sample as it's finding it. So, they're automated. It's not something that somebody has to sit there and comb through a bunch of images as it's taking these x-ray slices and say, okay, that looks like a void that shouldn't be there. It's finding it in real time without the operator having to intervene at all. extraction.body: Dr. Linir Zamir, who’s been working on the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite, discusses how Artificial Intelligence is re-shaping manufacturing. AI is moving fast, and on the factory floor, that speed brings both excitement and real concern. Some workers worry it’s going to replace them. Others are interested, but hesitant, because they’ve heard about hallucinations, bad outputs and AI tools that sound great in theory but fall apart in real operations. In this conversation, we focus on the practical side: how people in the AI industry are working to make these systems more reliable, how manufacturers can use AI to strengthen the workforce they already have and what it actually looks like to deploy AI across the factory floor in a way that delivers return on investment. ASSEMBLY: Folks are fearful of AI taking over their jobs. From your perspective, what’s the most realistic way workers should think about AI? And what advice would you give to someone who’s worried it’s going to replace them? ZAMIR: It makes sense to be cautious about AI. I understand it. You hear it all over. You’ve seen the movies, and the idea of AI can be terrifying sometimes. But I think nowadays, as time progresses and we see more and more AI evolving within our daily lives—like ChatGPT—people are now using it for almost anything, even drafting an email. You can use ChatGPT. ChatGPT does not send the email, but it does help you draft a better version of it. That’s exactly the same way we think about agents in manufacturing. We’re not replacing the operator. We’re not taking the job from them. We’re giving the operator the tools to make better decisions, to understand the procedure better, and to have the right context whenever they need it. Every evolution has some cautiousness and fearfulness related to it, and it’s the same with AI. But it’s something that the more we understand, the less we’re afraid of it. We’re giving the operators—and any level of the manufacturer—the tools, but we also explain how the tool behaves. What exactly does it do? What data is being transferred between the different agents? So we don’t give just the tool by itself, but also a deeper understanding of what exactly is happening, so people can understand it and not be afraid of it. And yeah. At the end of the day, we are not replacing; we are enhancing. ASSEMBLY: In the recent past, AI has been criticized for a number of reasons. How do folks in the AI industry tackle these issues to make sure the AI agents are as foolproof as they can be? ZAMIR: I think there are two points to what you said. One of them is that up until recently, AI had the issue of what is called hallucination, where it was not as reliable. People found errors or issues. There was a famous example with ChatGPT and the number of “R’s” in the word “strawberry.” I don’t know if you’ve heard of that, but ChatGPT hallucinated 30% to 40% of the time. If we are trying to build agents for manufacturers, where every second counts and accuracy is critical, we cannot allow those hallucinations. But in the past year or so, we’ve seen tools—and the foundation models themselves—become as reliable as you can get, assuming you give them the right context, which is what we do with the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite. We provide the right context. And there’s going to be pushback on any new technology. ASSEMBLY: That’s a very good point about pushback. How do you handle that when you talk to manufacturers? ZAMIR: First of all, the quality of the language models is much better than it used to be. We are in a very close relationship with NVIDIA, as mentioned, and we are implementing some foundation models. For example, Cosmos. Cosmos is a foundation model that is designed to be specific for manufacturing, so it has a much better understanding of the environment. That’s one thing. But hallucination depends on the context that you provide to the agent, because deviceWISE has so much data. So for any question or any understanding the agent needs, we provide the proper context. And we also have MCP protocol, which allows us to provide the agents with exactly the right context they need in order to understand, make a decision, and provide the right result or output to the operator for any input it might get. Those are the ways we can essentially fix, or handle, cases of hallucination. I would say this is 99.9% hallucination-proof, but for the 0.01%, that’s why you still have the person. That’s why we still need the person to validate and to say, “That’s true,” or “Holds up. It’s not an issue like you think it is.” But having this person is a layer of protection. The longer you have the agent running, and the longer it can interact with a person and understand the context of the environment it resides in, the less chance there is of it making any mistake or hallucination. So yeah: the quality of the agent, the MCP or the context involved, and then the person at the end to verify that everything is accurate. That’s part of it. Like all agentic AI, there’s going to be pushback, but the way we solve that and make people believe in the technology is to show them. We are comfortable with what we bring. We know what we have, and we’ve seen success all around. Being able to put the technology on the factory floor—bringing the small hardware component that can suddenly see everything—and showing them, “Hey, listen, within a minute I can see all the temperature changes, and I can give you an evaluation of what might fault within the next week or month,” and giving them this data shows the value. Initially, they might push back a little, but once they see the results they expect to see, it becomes much easier to adopt those technologies. At the end of the day, it’s a question of money, like almost everything is. If we can help manufacturers lower cost and lower downtime—which costs them a lot of money—they will definitely be inclined to adopt that technology and use the new tools that are available nowadays. Ask ASM → ASSEMBLY: A lot of manufacturers, because of the skilled labor shortage, are having to take the teams that they already have and make the most of them. This idea of using AI to enhance the operator basically means giving the people on the plant floor tools that help them work faster, make better decisions, and solve problems more consistently, without replacing their expertise or taking them out of the process, right? ZAMIR: Yeah, definitely. And what you said, we’ve heard so many times before. Actually, even NVIDIA themselves brought this up the other day when we had a conversation with them. ASSEMBLY: Can you explain how AI programs like the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite fit into this idea? ZAMIR: The Intelligence Suite helps exactly with that situation. We can take the operator, and we can even help with the training of an operator. Instead of spending hours and taking time from other operators to teach or explain, you can have the Intelligence Suite as the source of knowledge that every operator can use to know more and to understand the process that needs to be taken, to be much more productive, to understand the concept of the factory much better, and to know exactly what steps need to be taken. So we definitely help with that specific issue that we’ve seen across all factories that we’ve worked with. ASSEMBLY: What ROI should manufacturers expect when deploying agents across the factory floor? ZAMIR: Definitely the most immediate one is downtime recovery, or time to recovery. This is by far the main focus area of what we do. We want to make sure to minimize any error or fault. And because deviceWISE Intelligence is located right between the OT we get from the robots and the IT data from the top, when you get a fault on one of the robots, deviceWISE Intelligence can immediately contact SAP or CMMS maintenance, and even order the part if needed, depending on the requirement from that manufacturer. So downtime can get significantly shorter, and that’s the goal of what we’re trying to do. That’s one of the main impacts we see. ASSEMBLY: And building on that, tell us about the idea of self-mapping factories. ZAMIR: Yeah, self-mapping factory is our vision where the software can see the factory as a living system. Instead of the engineer needing to configure every connection, if you want to swap something like a piece of hardware, it’s a process. This self-mapping factory is going to identify different PLCs, robots and sensors, and it can help you see exactly the effect of different changes you might have. We also have what is called a digital twin as part of the Intelligence Suite, which allows us to have a simulation of the real-life factory you have, where you have all the different components like the PLCs, sensors and robots. All of them reside on a digital twin that lets you see the effect of anything you might change in the real factory. In the real-life factory, if I want to add another conveyor belt, is the robot movement going to hit it by mistake? Those are questions you would not know until you tried it yourself in the real factory. Instead of doing that—where you need to buy the parts and take risks—now you can do the simulation and see how it behaves. Now you have the self-mapping factory in real life and in the simulation. It can oversee all the data it has, all the context of the factory, including the components, the location, the distances, the temperature and all of those pieces of information can be leveraged by the Intelligence Suite to find the connection between different things, or different parts, that you have in the factory. This is essentially the factory of the future. Every factory is going to eventually get to that point. You want to have a simulation of your factory so you can cut costs tremendously, and test different scenarios and replacements within this digital simulation. ASSEMBLY: How many factories are using digital twins at this moment? ZAMIR: Honestly, at first I thought it was, “Oh, it’s a cool thing to have.” It sounds nice. We were like, “Okay, let’s see. How can we integrate that? What can we do?” But the response was incredible. I would say eight out of 10 large manufacturers that we work with have some sort of digital twin implementation, and it is being adopted like crazy at so many different levels. We’ve seen factories benefit so much from those digital twins, to be able, like I mentioned, to see all the different scenarios that might occur. Everything is a question of money at the end of the day. If this digital twin can help factories lower cost because they don’t need to take chances—they can simulate everything before they act in real life—it’s cost saving. We’ve seen it adopted a lot. ASSEMBLY: While a lot of manufacturers have adopted AI at some level, a lot don’t have any deployment across the factory floor. So what advice do you have for manufacturing leaders who are looking to scale, and how does deviceWISE help with this issue in particular? ZAMIR: Again, very good question. AI is such a big umbrella. There are so many components that can be labeled as AI. There are so many options for implementing AI. The question is: what is the AI that you work with? From a high-level perspective, what we do is integrations with deviceWISE. Part of the integration is integrations with AI tools and components, which is why we are working closely with NVIDIA. But not just NVIDIA—we work with different NPU manufacturers as well. This is part of the reason we have MCP: to be more agnostic to the AI being used or deployed in different manufacturers. So I would say integrations are the key part. ASSEMBLY: A lot of folks in manufacturing are retiring or getting close to retiring. What advice do you have to manufacturing leaders who are looking for candidates to fill those roles, especially given this AI emergence? ZAMIR: Definitely, I would say the younger generation is more technology-friendly, or savvy. It’s not a requirement, but it definitely helps. It can help the operator when interacting with those different agents. We’ve done work with many factories, and the people we worked with who interacted with deviceWISE and the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite are close to retirement age. But it’s essentially like talking to ChatGPT. Even my parents use ChatGPT, and they’re close to retiring, and they can still use it. It’s easy. It’s very intuitive, it’s interactive, and you don’t need to be as technology-savvy to work with those different agents. It’s the same for the factory. So while it does help if you know a little bit more about the technology, it’s not a requirement. You can have an agent you talk to, as we’re talking right now. You can talk to the agent, and it can provide you with information in a friendly way. It can be an Excel sheet, a PDF or whatever, that you can go over and read. So yeah, it’s not a requirement. It’s good, but we want to make it as simple and intuitive as possible to interact with those different agents. Looking for a reprint of this article? Instead of spending hours and taking time from other operators to teach or explain, you can have the Intelligence Suite as the source of knowledge that every operator can use to know more and to understand the process that needs to be taken, to be much more productive, to understand the concept of the factory much better, and to know exactly what steps need to be taken. So we definitely help with that specific issue that we’ve seen across all factories that we’ve worked with.
ASSEMBLY: What ROI should manufacturers expect when deploying agents across the factory floor?

ZAMIR: Definitely the most immediate one is downtime recovery, or time to recovery. This is by far the main focus area of what we do. We want to make sure to minimize any error or fault. And because deviceWISE Intelligence is located right between the OT we get from the robots and the IT data from the top, when you get a fault on one of the robots, deviceWISE Intelligence can immediately contact SAP or CMMS maintenance, and even order the part if needed, depending on the requirement from that manufacturer. So downtime can get significantly shorter, and that’s the goal of what we’re trying to do. That’s one of the main impacts we see.
ASSEMBLY: And building on that, tell us about the idea of self-mapping factories.

ZAMIR: Yeah, self-mapping factory is our vision where the software can see the factory as a living system. Instead of the engineer needing to configure every connection, if you want to swap something like a piece of hardware, it’s a process. This self-mapping factory is going to identify different PLCs, robots and sensors, and it can help you see exactly the effect of different changes you might have. We also have what is called a digital twin as part of the Intelligence Suite, which allows us to have a simulation of the real-life factory you have, where you have all the different components like the PLCs, sensors and robots. All of them reside on a digital twin that lets you see the effect of anything you might change in the real factory. In the real-life factory, if I want to add another conveyor belt, is the robot movement going to hit it by mistake? Those are questions you would not know until you tried it yourself in the real factory. Instead of doing that—where you need to buy the parts and take risks—now you can do the simulation and see how it behaves. Now you have the self-mapping factory in real life and in the simulation. It can oversee all the data it has, all the context of the factory, including the components, the location, the distances, the temperature and all of those pieces of information can be leveraged by the Intelligence Suite to find the connection between different things, or different parts, that you have in the factory. This is essentially the factory of the future. Every factory is going to eventually get to that point. You want to have a simulation of your factory so you can cut costs tremendously, and test different scenarios and replacements within this digital simulation.
ASSEMBLY: How many factories are using digital twins at this moment?

ZAMIR: Honestly, at first I thought it was, “Oh, it’s a cool thing to have.” It sounds nice. We were like, “Okay, let’s see. How can we integrate that? What can we do?” But the response was incredible. I would say eight out of 10 large manufacturers that we work with have some sort of digital twin implementation, and it is being adopted like crazy at so many different levels. We’ve seen factories benefit so much from those digital twins, to be able, like I mentioned, to see all the different scenarios that might occur. Everything is a question of money at the end of the day. If this digital twin can help factories lower cost because they don’t need to take chances—they can simulate everything before they act in real life—it’s cost saving. We’ve seen it adopted a lot.

ASSEMBLY: While a lot of manufacturers have adopted AI at some level, a lot don’t have any deployment across the factory floor. So what advice do you have for manufacturing leaders who are looking to scale, and how does deviceWISE help with this issue in particular?

ZAMIR: Again, very good question. AI is such a big umbrella. There are so many components that can be labeled as AI. There are so many options for implementing AI. The question is: what is the AI that you work with? From a high-level perspective, what we do is integrations with deviceWISE. Part of the integration is integrations with AI tools and components, which is why we are working closely with NVIDIA. But not just NVIDIA—we work with different NPU manufacturers as well. This is part of the reason we have MCP: to be more agnostic to the AI being used or deployed in different manufacturers. So I would say integrations are the key part.

ASSEMBLY: A lot of folks in manufacturing are retiring or getting close to retiring. What advice do you have to manufacturing leaders who are looking for candidates to fill those roles, especially given this AI emergence?

ZAMIR: Definitely, I would say the younger generation is more technology-friendly, or savvy. It’s not a requirement, but it definitely helps. It can help the operator when interacting with those different agents. We’ve done work with many factories, and the people we worked with who interacted with deviceWISE and the deviceWISE Intelligence Suite are close to retirement age. But it’s essentially like talking to ChatGPT. Even my parents use ChatGPT, and they’re close to retiring, and they can still use it. It’s easy. It’s very intuitive, it’s interactive, and you don’t need to be as technology-savvy to work with those different agents. It’s the same for the factory. So while it does help if you know a little bit more about the technology, it’s not a requirement. You can have an agent you talk to, as we’re talking right now. You can talk to the agent, and it can provide you with information in a friendly way. It can be an Excel sheet, a PDF or whatever, that you can go over and read. So yeah, it’s not a requirement. It’s good, but we want to make it as simple and intuitive as possible to interact with those different agents.

coreStoryFacts.text: The United States Director of National Intelligence, Jay Clayton, seemingly confirmed that China gained access to some of the US's advanced AI chips with restricted access.China's access to US-made restricted AI chips has become a major talking point following the fallout from ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

But the most comprehensive account of the network that Alice Huang operated in emerged from a report by The Financial Times published on November 21.The report revealed how Nvidia chips allegedly were diverted to China purportedly through a network of Chinese gaming companies, intermediaries in Southeast Asia, shell companies and a criminal network in Cambodia.It claimed that a Malaysian subsidiary of Megaspeed, Speedmatrix, imported chips worth $4.6 billion from Aivres, one of Nvidia's US-based manufacturers.

passages: The race for faster data processing is pushing infrastructure to its limits, forcing a choice between specialized connectivity and massive storage.
You might be deciding between Credo Technology Group (NASDAQ:CRDO) and Western Digital (NASDAQ:WDC) for 2027.
The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.

Credo provides high-speed connectivity solutions that enable artificial intelligence data centers to communicate efficiently, while Western Digital is a global leader in both hard disk and flash storage.
While they operate in different niches, both are essential players in the scaling of cloud infrastructure.
This comparison evaluates which stock offers the best path for long-term growth.
The company sells products like Active Electrical Cables and optical components to hyperscale operators and system vendors.
It has established key partnerships with Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) to enhance connectivity for dual-architecture systems.
The company also deals with geopolitical risks due to its reliance on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company for all semiconductor manufacturing.
Furthermore, it manages previously flagged intellectual property litigation with Marvell Technology, which was recently resolved via a settlement.

Western Digital designs and supplies essential data-storage solutions for enterprises and hyperscale cloud providers.
Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk, with three individual clients accounting for 16%, 15%, and 13% of total net revenue in its latest annual report.
To its credit, Western Digital's hard drives store much of the data AI creates, and its profit has jumped.
But rival Toshiba is reportedly doubling its hard drive capacity, which could pull prices down.
With plenty of cash on hand, it can keep investing in new products for years to come.
Western Digital must navigate risks associated with its complex strategic initiatives, such as the 2025 separation of its former flash business unit.
It competes directly with other storage manufacturers like Seagate Technology Holdings (NASDAQ:STX) and providers of alternative storage technologies.
Additionally, the company relies on a limited supply base for critical components, leaving it exposed to potential global supply chain disruptions.

The race for faster data processing is pushing infrastructure to its limits, forcing a choice between specialized connectivity and massive storage. You might be deciding between Credo Technology Group (NASDAQ:CRDO) and Western Digital (NASDAQ:WDC) for 2027. Credo provides high-speed connectivity solutions that enable artificial intelligence data centers to communicate efficiently, while Western Digital is a global leader in both hard disk and flash storage. While they operate in different niches, both are essential players in the scaling of cloud infrastructure. This comparison evaluates which stock offers the best path for long-term growth. Credo Technology Group specializes in high-speed copper and optical interconnect solutions designed for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The company sells products like Active Electrical Cables and optical components to hyperscale operators and system vendors. It has established key partnerships with Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) to enhance connectivity for dual-architecture systems. The demand for faster semiconductor stocks has significantly boosted its financial performance. In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue reached nearly $1.6 billion, representing a 165.1% increase over the previous period. This expansion led to a net income of roughly $538.3 million and a net margin of about 33.8%. As of its May 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0x, meaning the company carries no debt relative to shareholder equity. Its current ratio is approximately 10.2x, indicating a strong ability to cover short-term debts with current assets. In the fiscal year ended May 2, 2026, free cash flow reached nearly $407.0 million, though stock-based compensation represented roughly 39.3% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement. Western Digital designs and supplies essential data-storage solutions for enterprises and hyperscale cloud providers. Its product portfolio includes both hard disk drives and flash-based storage serving a global market across Asia and the Americas. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk, with three individual clients accounting for 16%, 15%, and 13% of total net revenue in its latest annual report. In the 12 months ended Oct. 2, 2026, revenue reached approximately $14.5 billion, representing a 43% increase compared to the prior year. Net income for this period was nearly $10.0 billion, which indicates a net margin of roughly 69.2%. This performance suggests a robust recovery in cloud storage demand, which now accounts for nearly 89% of its net revenue. On its July 2026 balance sheet, the company shows a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.1x, meaning total debt is low relative to equity. The current ratio stands at approximately 1.3x, measuring how well the company meets its short-term financial obligations. In the fiscal year ended July 3, 2026, free cash flow reached nearly $3.5 billion, representing operating cash flow minus capital expenditures. Credo Technology Group faces intense competition from larger industry peers like Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO), Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL), and Astera Labs (NASDAQ:ALAB). The company also deals with geopolitical risks due to its reliance on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company for all semiconductor manufacturing. Furthermore, it manages previously flagged intellectual property litigation with Marvell Technology, which was recently resolved via a settlement. Western Digital must navigate risks associated with its complex strategic initiatives, such as the 2025 separation of its former flash business unit. It competes directly with other storage manufacturers like Seagate Technology Holdings (NASDAQ:STX) and providers of alternative storage technologies. Additionally, the company relies on a limited supply base for critical components, leaving it exposed to potential global supply chain disruptions. Western Digital is cheaper, trading at a lower Forward P/E for future earnings estimates and a lower P/S ratio based on sales over the past twelve months. Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers. I'd go with Credo Technology, a company whose sales have more than doubled year over year for seven straight quarters. AI data centers run on thousands of chips that need to share data quickly, and Credo is a key player that makes the connections between them. Management expects sales to grow more than 85% this fiscal year, and Credo is also very profitable, turning about half of its sales into adjusted profit. It's also moving into optical products that carry data farther than its copper cables can, and management expects them to bring in more than $600 million this fiscal year. The stock fell after its recent earnings report, as investors worried that a few big customers make up most of its sales, but Credo added another big customer in its latest quarter. To its credit, Western Digital's hard drives store much of the data AI creates, and its profit has jumped. But rival Toshiba is reportedly doubling its hard drive capacity, which could pull prices down. For long-term investors, Credo pairs fast growth with strong profits, and it has a front-row seat as AI data centers get bigger. With plenty of cash on hand, it can keep investing in new products for years to come. Currently, Bitcoin trades around $60,763, 51.8% below its all-time high of $126,080 set on October 6, 2025. In its latest 24-hour session, its price moved between $58,696 and $61,447.

Bitcoin’s decline has been long and significant. Market analyst Charlie Bilello pointed out on November 21, 2026, that Bitcoin had dropped 56% from its peak to its low, marking the longest peak-to-trough decline in its history and lasting 411 days.

Despite this downturn, the $1 million target continues to generate interest. Bernstein, a Wall Street research firm, has set a long-term target of about $1 million by 2033, and long-term holders often cite it as a potential destination for Bitcoin. So, can Bitcoin still reach $1 million by 2035?

Market capitalization is the total value of a cryptocurrency, calculated by multiplying its price by the number of coins in circulation. If Bitcoin reached $1 million per coin, its market value would soar to around $20.12 trillion, up from about $1.22 trillion now. This required gain of 1,546% translates to an annual increase of roughly 36% over the 9.1 years remaining until the end of 2035.

Bitcoin’s growing supply adds another layer of difficulty to this target. When Bitcoin closed at $8,118 on November 22, 2017, its entire market cap was about $135.5 billion. Now, with approximately 20.1 million coins in circulation out of a maximum of 21 million, every dollar increase in price adds significantly more value than it did in 2017.

Reaching a market cap of $20.12 trillion would put Bitcoin in the same league as gold, a comparison supporters often use. However, gold is currently trading around $3,536 per ounce, down 33% from $5,279 at the end of February 2026, suggesting this benchmark has also declined.

Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) hold Bitcoin, so their purchases pull coins off the market. SoSoValue data indicates that cumulative net inflows to spot Bitcoin ETFs fell from $57.62 billion on October 29 to $53.51 billion on November 19.

On November 19 alone, these funds recorded $582 million in net outflows, and they took in money on only six trading days between October 23 and November 19. passages: For Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) to reach $1 million by 2035, it must gain about 1,546%. Over the past year, this goal has become even harder to reach. Currently, Bitcoin trades around $60,763, 51.8% below its all-time high of $126,080 set on October 6, 2025. In its latest 24-hour session, its price moved between $58,696 and $61,447.

Bitcoin’s decline has been long and significant. Market analyst Charlie Bilello pointed out on November 21, 2026, that Bitcoin had dropped 56% from its peak to its low, marking the longest peak-to-trough decline in its history and lasting 411 days.

Despite this downturn, the $1 million target continues to generate interest. Bernstein, a Wall Street research firm, has set a long-term target of about $1 million by 2033, and long-term holders often cite it as a potential destination for Bitcoin. So, can Bitcoin still reach $1 million by 2035?

Market capitalization is the total value of a cryptocurrency, calculated by multiplying its price by the number of coins in circulation. If Bitcoin reached $1 million per coin, its market value would soar to around $20.12 trillion, up from about $1.22 trillion now. This required gain of 1,546% translates to an annual increase of roughly 36% over the 9.1 years remaining until the end of 2035.

Bitcoin’s growing supply adds another layer of difficulty to this target. When Bitcoin closed at $8,118 on November 22, 2017, its entire market cap was about $135.5 billion. Now, with approximately 20.1 million coins in circulation out of a maximum of 21 million, every dollar increase in price adds significantly more value than it did in 2017.

Reaching a market cap of $20.12 trillion would put Bitcoin in the same league as gold, a comparison supporters often use. However, gold is currently trading around $3,536 per ounce, down 33% from $5,279 at the end of February 2026, suggesting this benchmark has also declined.

Bernstein bases its projections on Bitcoin’s four-year cycle, which is linked to the halving, an event that reduces the reward for mining new coins roughly every four years. Under Bernstein’s main scenario, Bitcoin could reach $150,000 by mid-2027, climb to about $300,000 in 2029, and near $1 million by 2033. However, this same report anticipated Bitcoin would rebound to $125,000 by late 2026, and Bitcoin is currently trading far below that level.

Standard Chartered has a more cautious outlook. The bank pushed its $500,000 target back from 2028 to 2030 in December 2025. In April 2026, analyst Geoffrey Kendrick set a year-end price target of $100,000. Even this $100,000 goal now seems ambitious.

Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) hold Bitcoin, so their purchases pull coins off the market. SoSoValue data indicates that cumulative net inflows to spot Bitcoin ETFs fell from $57.62 billion on October 29 to $53.51 billion on November 19.

On November 19 alone, these funds recorded $582 million in net outflows, and they took in money on only six trading days between October 23 and November 19. The total net assets of Bitcoin ETFs dropped to $76.55 billion from $104.88 billion on October 28, squeezed by both outflows and declining prices.

Higher interest rates add more pressure. The federal funds rate is the benchmark for overnight loans, and higher rates typically divert investment away from speculative assets like Bitcoin. The Federal Reserve raised its upper limit to 4.00% from 3.75% in September, and markets are bracing for another possible rate hike on December 9. Kendrick has cautioned that if this tightening continues, Bitcoin could drop to about $50,000, 18% below its current price.

Since it closed at $8,118 in November 2017, Bitcoin has grown at an annual compounded rate of about 25%. While this is a strong performance for most assets, it falls short of the 36% annual growth needed to reach the $1 million target.

The last five years have shown even weaker performance. Bitcoin has risen only about 4% since November 2021, despite nearly an 8,000% increase over the past decade. Both our five-year Bitcoin outlook and our look at $1,000 in Bitcoin by 2030 illustrate how much returns have slowed.

Even Bitcoin enthusiasts predict more modest gains going forward. Investor and podcast host Anthony Pompliano remarked on August 19, 2026, “The future return of Bitcoin, I think, is going to be much lower than people have previously experienced. So I don’t think it’s going to compound at 60%, 70% year over year for a decade.”

Bitcoin’s chance of reaching $1 million by 2035 appears low. First, it must recover its all-time high of $126,080, which is 107% above the current price, as our prediction on when Bitcoin gets back there covers. Then spot ETF outflows need to turn into steady inflows, the Fed needs to stop raising rates, and Bitcoin has to compound near 36% a year, faster than it has since 2017.

Bernstein’s $150,000 mid-2027 checkpoint is the first test. If Bitcoin is still below $126,080 by mid-2027 and cumulative ETF inflows keep shrinking from $53.51 billion, the $1 million target could slip well past 2035. But if Bitcoin closes above its old high with weeks of steady ETF inflows, $1 million could return to serious conversation, though the late 2030s still look more likely.

passages: The security table runs from DSA-6408 to DSA-6629 (a DSA is a Debian Security Advisory).
It covers Chromium, Firefox ESR, OpenJDK 25, nginx, BIND 9, Dovecot, rsync, PostgreSQL 17 and the Linux kernel.
Chromium is the package the table lists most often.
A second table lists 122 packages with bugfixes, among them security fixes in glibc, grub2, MariaDB, intel-microcode and sssd.
The Debian project released Debian 13.8, the eighth update to its stable “trixie” series.
It mainly carries security fixes, plus corrections for a few serious bugs, and it bundles advisories Debian had already published separately.
Existing installs get 13.8 by upgrading packages from an HTTP mirror , and old trixie install media still works.
If you already pull updates from security.debian.org often, you will find few packages left to update, since most of those fixes are already in the release.

passages: macOS offers one of the most refined desktop experiences, but users looking for more granular control of their desktops might find the OS' native options limiting.

Unlike Microsoft's PowerToys , which includes a collection of over 25 productivity and customization tools, Mac users must often turn to a fragmented selection of third-party applications to achieve similar levels of control.
For example, macOS' native window tiling is serviceable at best, allowing for only a few tiling options regardless of screen size.
Similarly, the OS doesn't natively support independent volume control and output device selection for individual applications.
This is where Vorssaint, the Swiss Army Knife of macOS utility apps, comes into the picture.
The application suite also includes several handy tools that streamline daily workflows.
For example, its screenshot utility supports scrolling screenshots, which makes it possible to capture content that extends beyond what's visible on the screen.
Users can also edit captured screenshots with the app's in-built image editing tool.
Similarly, Vorssaint's media tool is capable of video compression, image conversion and text extraction from images.
Meanwhile, its system monitoring tool extends beyond Mac's Activity Monitor, providing valuable information on thermals, memory usage and network speed.

Its functionality extends beyond just searching apps and files; it can also be used to perform quick mathematical calculations, unit conversions and access most of Vorssaint's utilities by simply searching for them.

For example, someone particularly interested in streamlining window management can choose to install only the Window layout module, and need not grant it screen recording and app management permissions.
This selective approach lets users retain the modules they without having to risk granting sensitive permissions.

extraction.body: Vorssaint is a powerful, modular utility suite, provided permissions are carefully managed. macOS offers one of the most refined desktop experiences, but users looking for more granular control of their desktops might find the OS' native options limiting. Unlike Microsoft's PowerToys , which includes a collection of over 25 productivity and customization tools, Mac users must often turn to a fragmented selection of third-party applications to achieve similar levels of control. For example, macOS' native window tiling is serviceable at best, allowing for only a few tiling options regardless of screen size. Similarly, the OS doesn't natively support independent volume control and output device selection for individual applications. This is where Vorssaint, the Swiss Army Knife of macOS utility apps, comes into the picture. Vorssaint is a third-party, open source application that aims to resolve macOS' productivity and customization pain points with a single menu-bar application. The app groups together a range of utility tools and nifty quick toggles to streamline productivity. The project is hosted on GitHub , and has earned over 33,000 stars and 230 contributors. Vorssaint includes an impressive collection of utilities that aims to improve how users interact with their Macs. Its window-tiling feature offers more control over how users arrange their application windows, including edge snapping and shortcuts. The app also includes a toggle for clamshell mode, enabling MacBooks to continue running even with their lids closed, while its "Keep Awake" feature allows users to control when or if their Macs can enter a sleep state. The application suite also includes several handy tools that streamline daily workflows. For example, its screenshot utility supports scrolling screenshots, which makes it possible to capture content that extends beyond what's visible on the screen. Users can also edit captured screenshots with the app's in-built image editing tool. Similarly, Vorssaint's media tool is capable of video compression, image conversion and text extraction from images. Meanwhile, its system monitoring tool extends beyond Mac's Activity Monitor, providing valuable information on thermals, memory usage and network speed. These are just a few examples of what Vorssaint offers. The suite also includes a graphical interface for Homebrew, URL cleaner and a powerful command bar. The command bar is akin to Apple's Spotlight search , but a lot more exciting. Its functionality extends beyond just searching apps and files; it can also be used to perform quick mathematical calculations, unit conversions and access most of Vorssaint's utilities by simply searching for them. Vorssaint's robust utility stack undoubtedly makes it a promising productivity suite for power users. However, some of its powerful tools require sensitive macOS permissions. Depending on what features users install, the app may request permissions for Accessibility, Screen Recording, Full Disk Access and Automation. While granting these permissions is necessary to allow Vorssaint to perform some of its functions like taking screenshots, uninstalling applications and other system-level operations, users must understand what it means to grant system-level permissions to applications, especially those built by third-party developers. This is where Vorssaint's modular design becomes particularly useful, allowing users to choose specific modules according to their requirements. For example, someone particularly interested in streamlining window management can choose to install only the Window layout module, and need not grant it screen recording and app management permissions. This selective approach lets users retain the modules they without having to risk granting sensitive permissions. Finally, according to Vorssaint's privacy documentation, the app emphasizes an open-source and local-first approach. It doesn't require users to set up an account, subscribe to a service or share usage analytics with the developer. However, it's worth noting that an application being open source does not validate its security. Therefore, users are advised to consider the app's privacy trade-off before choosing to install it on their Macs.

Lauren covers media, streaming, apps and platforms at TechCrunch.
The app uses a paid membership model that varies by city, with fees of $70 in New York and €55 in Amsterdam.
The apps aim to provide a less awkward solution than, for instance, approaching a stranger at the gym or local café and trying to strike up a conversation.
These platforms clearly indicate that everyone using the app is looking for the same thing — friendship, not romance — making it much less intimidating to initiate conversations.
The app 222 is an iOS-only social events platform that facilitates in-person meetups by pairing a group of strangers based on their personality test results.
There is then a vetting process, and selected participants are notified on the day of the event.
A bonus for those who feel socially anxious: You’re allowed to bring a plus-one.
Clyx is another emerging app in the group-based social networking landscape, with a strong focus on discovering local events.
The social platform helps users find community events by integrating data from platforms like Ticketmaster and TikTok.
They can also chat with group members and post updates and photos from gatherings.
Mmotion is a newly launched friendship app that blends location tracking with social discovery to help users connect with people nearby and explore new bars and restaurants in their area.
Upon joining, users can participate in interest-based groups — such as hiking, basketball, or art — view a map of active users, and send messages to those nearby.
As of now, Clyx operates exclusively in two cities: Miami and London.
However, it has plans to expand to additional areas in the near future, with New York City and São Paulo at the top of the list.

extraction.body: In recent years, people have been increasingly looking for new ways to form platonic connections, as loneliness and social isolation have become more prevalent. In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General went so far as to label this issue a public health crisis. Remote workers, who miss the everyday interactions found in an office, and younger individuals eager to create their adult social circles based on shared interests and hobbies, are among those seeking meaningful friendships. Thanks to online dating apps, the stigma associated with finding connections online has largely faded away. This has welcomed a new wave of apps focused on fostering friendships and building local communities. According to estimates from Appfigures, over a dozen local-focused friendship apps have collectively generated approximately $16 million in consumer spending in the U.S. so far this year. Some notable examples include Timeleft, Meet5, and Bumble’s BFF. Additionally, these apps have garnered approximately 4.3 million downloads thus far in 2025. The apps aim to provide a less awkward solution than, for instance, approaching a stranger at the gym or local café and trying to strike up a conversation. These platforms clearly indicate that everyone using the app is looking for the same thing — friendship, not romance — making it much less intimidating to initiate conversations. From major players like Meetup to newer ones like 222, there are plenty of apps that cater to the growing demand for meaningful friendships. We’ve compiled a list of them for you to try out. The app 222 is an iOS-only social events platform that facilitates in-person meetups by pairing a group of strangers based on their personality test results. The app sends invitations to nearby public social events, such as wine bars and comedy clubs. There is then a vetting process, and selected participants are notified on the day of the event. A bonus for those who feel socially anxious: You’re allowed to bring a plus-one. BFF is available for free download on iOS and Android devices. Clyx is another emerging app in the group-based social networking landscape, with a strong focus on discovering local events. The social platform helps users find community events by integrating data from platforms like Ticketmaster and TikTok. Additionally, Clyx allows users to upload their contact lists, helping them see which events their friends plan to attend. The app also includes a feature that recommends other users to connect with at these events. As of now, Clyx operates exclusively in two cities: Miami and London. However, it has plans to expand to additional areas in the near future, with New York City and São Paulo at the top of the list. The app is available on the App Store and Google Play Store . Crowdier is a new group social app that lets friend groups connect with others. Users can create a group of 2-5 friends and browse other groups to arrange hangouts in person. To initiate a match, users can “Wave” at groups they like, and if those groups wave back, they can plan in a shared chat. A match requires the majority of both groups to agree. For example, 2 people in a 4-person group needs to say yes. Available on iOS and Android , Les Amís serves cities across Europe, including Amsterdam, Barcelona, Berlin, Madrid, Paris, and Stockholm. In the U.S., the app is available in Austin and New York, with plans to expand to Boston, Miami, and Los Angeles. The app uses a paid membership model that varies by city, with fees of $70 in New York and €55 in Amsterdam. The local event-discovery platform has been around since 2002, helping millions of users connect with others who share similar interests. Users can RSVP to events; join groups that cater to a variety of hobbies, professions, or social causes; and create their own groups and events. They can also chat with group members and post updates and photos from gatherings. This European community-building app recently launched in the U.S., targeting users over 40 who want to meet new people in their area and participate in group activities such as picnics, concerts, and hiking. Notably, in a short time, there have been around 777,000 U.S. downloads so far across the App Store and Google Play Store , according to Appfigures estimates. Pie is another one of the newer social apps on the market. It features an AI-driven quiz designed to predict which users are most likely to be compatible with each other. Each person who RSVPs to a Pie event takes a brief personality assessment, and the algorithm organizes attendees into groups of six, who are then added to a group chat within the Pie app, allowing them to interact with each other before the event. Users can book dinners online or through the app . In terms of pricing, it varies depending on the country and restaurant. Users pay for a ticket up front and are responsible for covering their own dinner and drinks. Washed Up is a social event discovery app that launched in early 2026, designed for people in the Los Angeles area who want an easier way to find things to do and meet new people. The app helps users discover local events, such as concerts, trivia nights, and comedy shows, while also giving them a built-in way to connect with others who plan to attend. Instead of going to events alone, users can create or join “plans,” which are small group meetups tied to specific events. Users can browse these plans and request to join, chat with the group, and add new friends, making it easier to show up to events with people rather than by themselves. It’s available to download on the App Store . Wyzr Friends is an activity-based friendship app designed for adults 40 and older, catering to empty nesters, those who are divorced, and other users seeking to connect with like-minded individuals. Users can thumbs up or down potential friends and arrange in-person activities based on shared interests, such as going to the movies or hiking. It’s available on iOS and Android devices in the U.S., Canada, Australia, Ireland, the Philippines, Singapore, and Mexico. Mmotion is a newly launched friendship app that blends location tracking with social discovery to help users connect with people nearby and explore new bars and restaurants in their area. Upon joining, users can participate in interest-based groups — such as hiking, basketball, or art — view a map of active users, and send messages to those nearby. The app also highlights new places on the map, making it easy to find a restaurant or venue to try. Mmotion is currently only available to users in New York City on iOS and Android devices. Users must first submit an application to be considered. Launched in March 2026, Synchrony is a new social app tailored for neurodivergent adults. Founded by a mother of a son on the autism spectrum, it aims to create a supportive community through features like interest-based matching and two-step identity verification. This ensures that users engage safely, as both a user and a trusted person must verify personal details and a photo ID during registration. A standout feature is Jesse, an optional AI communication tool that assists users in navigating conversations. The AI provides editable prompts to help express thoughts, clarifies conversations, and offers boundary-setting suggestions. While the incorporation of AI may raise concerns, there are guardrails built into Jesse, such as avoiding medical advice. extraction.body: In recent years, people have been increasingly looking for new ways to form platonic connections, as loneliness and social isolation have become more prevalent. In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General went so far as to label this issue a public health crisis. Remote workers, who miss the everyday interactions found in an office, and younger individuals eager to create their adult social circles based on shared interests and hobbies, are among those seeking meaningful friendships. Thanks to online dating apps, the stigma associated with finding connections online has largely faded away. This has welcomed a new wave of apps focused on fostering friendships and building local communities. According to estimates from Appfigures, over a dozen local-focused friendship apps have collectively generated approximately $16 million in consumer spending in the U.S. so far this year. Some notable examples include Timeleft, Meet5, and Bumble’s BFF. Additionally, these apps have garnered approximately 4.3 million downloads thus far in 2025. The apps aim to provide a less awkward solution than, for instance, approaching a stranger at the gym or local café and trying to strike up a conversation. These platforms clearly indicate that everyone using the app is looking for the same thing — friendship, not romance — making it much less intimidating to initiate conversations. From major players like Meetup to newer ones like 222, there are plenty of apps that cater to the growing demand for meaningful friendships. We’ve compiled a list of them for you to try out. The app 222 is an iOS-only social events platform that facilitates in-person meetups by pairing a group of strangers based on their personality test results. The app sends invitations to nearby public social events, such as wine bars and comedy clubs. There is then a vetting process, and selected participants are notified on the day of the event. A bonus for those who feel socially anxious: You’re allowed to bring a plus-one. BFF is available for free download on iOS and Android devices. Clyx is another emerging app in the group-based social networking landscape, with a strong focus on discovering local events. The social platform helps users find community events by integrating data from platforms like Ticketmaster and TikTok. Additionally, Clyx allows users to upload their contact lists, helping them see which events their friends plan to attend. The app also includes a feature that recommends other users to connect with at these events. As of now, Clyx operates exclusively in two cities: Miami and London. However, it has plans to expand to additional areas in the near future, with New York City and São Paulo at the top of the list. The app is available on the App Store and Google Play Store . Crowdier is a new group social app that lets friend groups connect with others. Users can create a group of 2-5 friends and browse other groups to arrange hangouts in person. To initiate a match, users can “Wave” at groups they like, and if those groups wave back, they can plan in a shared chat. A match requires the majority of both groups to agree. For example, 2 people in a 4-person group needs to say yes. Available on iOS and Android , Les Amís serves cities across Europe, including Amsterdam, Barcelona, Berlin, Madrid, Paris, and Stockholm. In the U.S., the app is available in Austin and New York, with plans to expand to Boston, Miami, and Los Angeles. The app uses a paid membership model that varies by city, with fees of $70 in New York and €55 in Amsterdam. The local event-discovery platform has been around since 2002, helping millions of users connect with others who share similar interests. Users can RSVP to events; join groups that cater to a variety of hobbies, professions, or social causes; and create their own groups and events. They can also chat with group members and post updates and photos from gatherings. This European community-building app recently launched in the U.S., targeting users over 40 who want to meet new people in their area and participate in group activities such as picnics, concerts, and hiking. Notably, in a short time, there have been around 777,000 U.S. downloads so far across the App Store and Google Play Store , according to Appfigures estimates. Pie is another one of the newer social apps on the market. It features an AI-driven quiz designed to predict which users are most likely to be compatible with each other. Each person who RSVPs to a Pie event takes a brief personality assessment, and the algorithm organizes attendees into groups of six, who are then added to a group chat within the Pie app, allowing them to interact with each other before the event. Users can book dinners online or through the app . In terms of pricing, it varies depending on the country and restaurant. Users pay for a ticket up front and are responsible for covering their own dinner and drinks. Washed Up is a social event discovery app that launched in early 2026, designed for people in the Los Angeles area who want an easier way to find things to do and meet new people. The app helps users discover local events, such as concerts, trivia nights, and comedy shows, while also giving them a built-in way to connect with others who plan to attend. Instead of going to events alone, users can create or join “plans,” which are small group meetups tied to specific events. Users can browse these plans and request to join, chat with the group, and add new friends, making it easier to show up to events with people rather than by themselves. It’s available to download on the App Store . Wyzr Friends is an activity-based friendship app designed for adults 40 and older, catering to empty nesters, those who are divorced, and other users seeking to connect with like-minded individuals. Users can thumbs up or down potential friends and arrange in-person activities based on shared interests, such as going to the movies or hiking. It’s available on iOS and Android devices in the U.S., Canada, Australia, Ireland, the Philippines, Singapore, and Mexico. Mmotion is a newly launched friendship app that blends location tracking with social discovery to help users connect with people nearby and explore new bars and restaurants in their area. Upon joining, users can participate in interest-based groups — such as hiking, basketball, or art — view a map of active users, and send messages to those nearby. The app also highlights new places on the map, making it easy to find a restaurant or venue to try. Mmotion is currently only available to users in New York City on iOS and Android devices. Users must first submit an application to be considered. Launched in March 2026, Synchrony is a new social app tailored for neurodivergent adults. Founded by a mother of a son on the autism spectrum, it aims to create a supportive community through features like interest-based matching and two-step identity verification. This ensures that users engage safely, as both a user and a trusted person must verify personal details and a photo ID during registration. A standout feature is Jesse, an optional AI communication tool that assists users in navigating conversations. The AI provides editable prompts to help express thoughts, clarifies conversations, and offers boundary-setting suggestions. While the incorporation of AI may raise concerns, there are guardrails built into Jesse, such as avoiding medical advice. sources.title: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
passages: Lilian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F.
Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment.

On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times.
Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors.
Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history.
But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its 2024 split from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future.

“We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch.
Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said.

Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times.
Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win.

Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption. GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation.

“Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch. “It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion. Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials.

Lilian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F. Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch.

After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said.

“It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added. Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations.

passages: One thing to mention about these apps is that, depending on your employer, restrictions may apply.
Certain companies require corporate apps like Google Meet and Microsoft Teams to run inside an isolated Android Work Profile.
In such situations, Android Auto may block calendar sync or prevent the app from appearing on the screen.
There's a Work Mode in the works on Android Auto , though, so it may soon be easier to reach all those apps that are locked out by your employer.
Because Meet is Google's own app, it fits naturally into the Android Auto experience.
You can see your upcoming meetings on the car display and join a call with a single tap, all in audio-only mode so your eyes stay on the road.
Whether it's a short check-in with your manager or a longer team call, Meet makes it easy to keep up with your schedule even if you have to drive around.
Yes, Android Auto will read out your texts — we all know that.
But it can also handle other apps, reading out your messages if you so desire and then letting you use your voice to reply.
WhatsApp is the clearest example of this working well, as Android Auto can read your messages aloud.
Signal offers similar read-aloud and reply functionality; so do Facebook Messenger, Microsoft Teams and Google Chat, to name a few.
But the platform's compatible app library runs much deeper, well beyond navigation and streaming.
Each one adds layer after layer of functionality that most users never think to explore.
Discovering new apps can genuinely change how you commute while also making it possible to enjoy your drive just a tiny bit more.
Google Maps and other similar tools can surface the nearest gas stations and even tell you the latest prices, but Fuelio gives more in-depth information regarding fuel type, distance and more.
While Fuelio is free to use with Android Auto, there is a premium version available that costs money.
When you're traveling abroad, costs go up by quite a bit, so you should make the most of your home Wi-Fi.
Apps like HERE WeGo through Android Auto offer offline navigation, so your data plan isn't ever a concern.
For some countries, you can download maps for certain areas, such as for Germany where you can grab a map for Berlin and another for Hamburg.
Compatible apps will automatically pop up on your Android Auto launcher.
This free tool (the paid version removes ads) gives you access to a crowd-sourced map that lets you see the nearest charging stations along your route.
Its real strength is the community behind it, because drivers leave real-time feedback, uploading photos of the charger layout, reporting broken plugs and checking in after charging.
That gives you a clear picture of what to expect before you pull in, so a station that looks fine on paper but has been out of service for days won't catch you off guard.

extraction.body: Some of these apps will be familiar, while others you may not have heard of. Android Auto users typically utilize just a few basic apps like Google Maps for directions and Spotify for music. They don't dive into the developer menu ; they don't make any serious changes to the way Android Auto works; and they don't know they could be spending all those minutes waiting for someone in a parking lot playing games directly on the car's infotainment display . But the platform's compatible app library runs much deeper, well beyond navigation and streaming. Android Auto actually supports a surprising range of communication and meeting tools, like WhatsApp and Google Meet, and even a bunch of other apps to help you navigate more efficiently. Each one adds layer after layer of functionality that most users never think to explore. Discovering new apps can genuinely change how you commute while also making it possible to enjoy your drive just a tiny bit more. Android Auto comes with some extra functionality for those in the corporate world, as several popular apps come with Android Auto support for meetings and calls, with Google Meet leading the way. Because Meet is Google's own app, it fits naturally into the Android Auto experience. You can see your upcoming meetings on the car display and join a call with a single tap, all in audio-only mode so your eyes stay on the road. Whether it's a short check-in with your manager or a longer team call, Meet makes it easy to keep up with your schedule even if you have to drive around. Google's app isn't the only option, though. Zoom, Webex by Cisco and Microsoft Teams all work on Android Auto, offering users the opportunity to join video conferences with audio only. Some apps take integration a step further. Microsoft Teams, for instance, lets users check their calendar and place calls directly from the car display. Google Meet also displays upcoming meetings on your schedule. These features are particularly useful if you're often traveling from location to location but still have to participate in meetings along the way. They also help if you have to leave early to pick up the kids from school while a meeting is still on your calendar. One thing to mention about these apps is that, depending on your employer, restrictions may apply. Certain companies require corporate apps like Google Meet and Microsoft Teams to run inside an isolated Android Work Profile. In such situations, Android Auto may block calendar sync or prevent the app from appearing on the screen. There's a Work Mode in the works on Android Auto , though, so it may soon be easier to reach all those apps that are locked out by your employer. With gas prices being what they are these days, it's more important than ever to know where to fuel up. Apps like Fuelio can help with that when you're looking for a place to put gas in your car without breaking the bank. Fuelio tracks fill-ups, odometer readings and fuel prices, then calculates your average fuel economy and cost per mile over time. You can even use various filters to display gas stations that were updated within the past day, or those that are most appreciated by users. Google Maps and other similar tools can surface the nearest gas stations and even tell you the latest prices, but Fuelio gives more in-depth information regarding fuel type, distance and more. Plus, when you throw in all the other features, it's a much better fit if you want to know exactly how much your car is costing you. While Fuelio is free to use with Android Auto, there is a premium version available that costs money. If you're driving an EV, then the app you absolutely must use through Android Auto is PlugShare . This free tool (the paid version removes ads) gives you access to a crowd-sourced map that lets you see the nearest charging stations along your route. Its real strength is the community behind it, because drivers leave real-time feedback, uploading photos of the charger layout, reporting broken plugs and checking in after charging. That gives you a clear picture of what to expect before you pull in, so a station that looks fine on paper but has been out of service for days won't catch you off guard. There are loads of filters you can play with, letting you choose the exact plug type, charging speed and network. You can also check which amenities are nearby, such as restrooms or a place to grab coffee while you wait. It's also a great tool for long-distance drives, as it automatically recommends charging stops along the way based on your specific EV model's range. That goes a long way toward easing the range anxiety that comes with getting an electric car. The one downside is that the data is only as good as its contributors, so stations in less-traveled areas may have fewer recent reports. Data can be expensive, especially if you use your phone a ton. When you're traveling abroad, costs go up by quite a bit, so you should make the most of your home Wi-Fi. Apps like HERE WeGo through Android Auto offer offline navigation, so your data plan isn't ever a concern. HERE WeGo lets you download maps for entire countries so you always know where you're going. For some countries, you can download maps for certain areas, such as for Germany where you can grab a map for Berlin and another for Hamburg. In the United States, you can grab maps for entire states, but not separate cities. There are plenty of features to fiddle with to make this app yours, like choosing which fuel type your car uses, having the metric vs. imperial system displayed the way you prefer and so on. The app will flag parking spots and rest areas along the route, and you can even tell it what types of things to avoid. For instance, Waze lets you avoid ferries and highways, but HERE WeGo can have you avoid tunnels and U-turns too. The app can take things one step further and even use visual references on route, which means it will tell you to make a right at the traffic light or when you reach a certain landmark. Yes, Android Auto will read out your texts — we all know that. But it can also handle other apps, reading out your messages if you so desire and then letting you use your voice to reply. WhatsApp is the clearest example of this working well, as Android Auto can read your messages aloud. Then, Gemini asks if you want to reply and will type out the words for you. Signal offers similar read-aloud and reply functionality; so do Facebook Messenger, Microsoft Teams and Google Chat, to name a few. This feature can be super useful when you're driving as you can stay connected without taking your eyes off the road. The ability to reply to messages will also help you stay on top of any emergencies without having to pull over. However, as with any AI typing tool, you should expect some mistakes here and there. Adding all these apps is straightforward as you only have to install them from the Google Play Store on your phone. Compatible apps will automatically pop up on your Android Auto launcher. You can go into the Android Auto settings and reorganize the apps if you want to make some more easily accessible. Android Auto's compatibility list is wider than most people assume, but the best setup prioritizes the tools that you actually use when you're behind the wheel.
